  • Delegates who are Authorized Representatives may also have authority in addition to that established using the Delegate Tools;
  • We will treat a Delegate appointment by one owner or certain Authorized Representatives of an Eligible Account as a Delegate appointment by all other owners of that Eligible Account;
  • View Only – Guest users and authorized users may have access to an Eligible Account or Online Financial Service, but only to view balance and transaction information and other non-transactional capabilities as permitted by the Service. If Delegate Tools are used by you to grant a guest user or authorized user with a username, password, or other login credential to access an Online Financial Service, you are responsible for any actions taken using your, your guest user, or authorized user's username and password; and
  • View and Transact – Authorized Representatives may have access to an Eligible Account or Online Financial Service, and may engage in and authorize specified transactions permitted by the Service.

If you make someone who is enrolled in the Service an authorized signer on an Eligible Account, we may treat that authorized signer as a Delegate and automatically assign View and Transact authority to that Delegate.

You agree that you may only appoint Delegates in accordance with the requirements we provide to you. This provision takes precedence over any conflicting provision in any other agreement you have with us. We may discontinue offering Delegate options or permitting Delegates to access your Eligible Account or Online Financial Services at any time, without prior notice.

Unless otherwise provided by law or regulation, an Authorized Representative or Delegate's transactions (including the transactions of their AI Agents) are considered authorized, unless (1) you tell us that they are no longer authorized as an Authorized Representative or Delegate, and (2) we have had reasonable opportunity to act on your notification.

For more details, please see the agreements for your Eligible Accounts and Online Financial Services.

A Delegate's authority will end when we have a reasonable opportunity to act on any of the following:

  • An owner of an Eligible Account or Authorized Representative lets us know that the Delegate's authority has ended and requests that the Delegate be removed.
  • An owner lets us know that the owner who appointed the Delegate is no longer an owner on the Eligible Account and requests that the Delegate be removed.

If you made a Delegate appointment through another area, you may need to follow the process for terminating the Delegate appointment through that same area to ensure all required actions are completed.

This provision controls and takes precedence over any conflicting provision in any other agreements you have with us.

3(a). Accessing Eligible Accounts and Online Financial Services

You authorize Wells Fargo to provide access to your Eligible Accounts and Online Financial Services through the Service. You may access your Eligible Accounts and Online Financial Services through the Website to obtain information and perform transactions authorized on the Website.

To access your Eligible Accounts and Online Financial Services through the Website, you need a username, a password, and required hardware and software (see Online Banking Help for details). To complete your enrollment in the Service, you will be required to validate your email address. Additionally, you are required to maintain an email address that is continuously operational to receive email communications from us in order to continue to access your Eligible Accounts and Online Financial Services through the Website. You must provide all computer, telephone and other equipment, software (other than any software provided by us), and services you need to access the Service. You must also comply with any other security procedures we may establish.

When using the Mobile Banking Service, you may generally access certain Eligible Accounts through the mobile browser, our mobile apps, or get certain information through text messaging or push notification on a Mobile Device. In order to do so, you must provide us with (and maintain) a valid mobile phone number, which you are the owner of or have the delegated legal authority to act on behalf of the mobile subscriber.

3(b). Account Linking and Display

Once you enroll for the Service, you can link and display certain Eligible Accounts. Eligible Accounts that are linked and displayed through the Mobile Banking Service may be subject to certain limitations and restrictions.

Eligible Accounts will appear on your Account Summary page on the Website without regard to who else may have an ownership interest in each Eligible Account.

3(c). Availability and Unavailability of Service

Subject to the terms of this Agreement, you'll generally be able to access your Eligible Accounts and Online Financial Services through the Website 24 hours per day, 7 days per week.

Sometimes the Service may be unavailable due to system maintenance or circumstances beyond our control. During these times, you may be able to call Online Customer Service at 1-800-956-4442, use a Wells Fargo ATM, or visit a Wells Fargo branch to obtain information about your Eligible Accounts. For brokerage accounts and services, contact your Financial Advisor, or call 1-877-879-2495 or 1-866-552-3312 (WFCS Custodied brokerage accounts).

3(d). Terminating Online Access

This Agreement will be in effect from the date we accept your enrollment in the Service and at all times while you're using the Service or any Online Financial Service.

Unless otherwise required by applicable law or regulation, either of us can terminate this Agreement and/or your access to any Eligible Account or Online Financial Service through the Service, in whole or in part, at any time. For example, we may terminate your access to the Services due to inactivity, at any time. We will try to notify you in advance of any termination, but are not required to do so.

We also may terminate access upon proper notification of death.

If you violate any terms of this Agreement (including non-payment of fees under any applicable fee schedule) or any other agreement you have with us, you agree that we may suspend or terminate your access to any of your Eligible Accounts and Online Financial Services. We are not required to reinstate or re-activate your access.

If you close all your Eligible Accounts, terminate your Online Financial Services, or withdraw from the Service, we may suspend or terminate your access without prior notification. We are not required to reinstate or re-activate your access. If reinstated, the then-current terms of this Agreement will control.

If you want to remove online access for an Eligible Account, you can do so through the Service or call:

  • Wells Fargo Online Customer Service at 1-800-956-4442
  • Wells Fargo Advisors accounts, call 1-877-879-2495 or 1-866-552-3312 (WFCS Custodied brokerage accounts)

If you have a Business Eligible Account or Business Online Financial Service, before authorizing access to the Service, we may require (based on terms, conditions, or other agreements) any Authorized Representative to enter into this Agreement, as amended.

4.  Electronic Fund Transfers Timing (General)

Unless the Website or our other agreements with you say otherwise, electronic fund transfers completed through the Service before the transfer cut-off time on a Business Day will be posted to your Eligible Account the same day. Credit card, line of credit, loan, and mortgage transactions may take up to three Business Days to process, but will post as of the Business Day the transaction was made.

All transfers completed after the transfer cut-off time on a Business Day, or on a day that is not a Business Day, will be posted on the next Business Day.

Please note that electronic fund transfers:

  • Between financial institutions will be processed, completed, and posted by the other institution following its own rules.
  • To and from brokerage accounts may have different transfer cut-off times or posting times.
  • Initiated through the Service for person-to-person payments may have different transfer cut-off or posting times.

For more information regarding instant payments, please see your Eligible Account agreement and the Bill Pay instant payments provisions in Section 6 below.

5(a). Applicability

The provisions in this Section apply only to electronic fund transfers (EFTs) that debit or credit a Consumer's checking, savings, or other asset account and are subject to Regulation E (subpart A), which implements the federal Electronic Fund Transfer Act.

When applicable, we may rely on any exceptions to the provisions in this Section that are covered in Regulation E. All terms in this Section not defined in this Agreement but defined in Regulation E will have the meaning given in Regulation E. For example, the term "unauthorized electronic fund transfer" (or unauthorized EFT) as used in this Section shall mean an electronic fund transfer from your account that is initiated by a person other than you without actual authority to initiate the transfer and from which you receive no benefit.

A transaction you initiate or otherwise authorize, even if induced to do so through fraud or deceit, is not considered an unauthorized electronic fund transfer for purposes of this Section. To learn about common scams and how to avoid them, please visit our online Security Center at www.wellsfargo.com/privacy-security/fraud/.

Note: Among other things, this Section does not apply to wire transfers that debit or credit a consumer’s account. This section does not apply to remittance transfers (e.g. ExpressSend® (or any successor product(s) we may offer from time to time) and consumer-initiated international wire transfers). For additional information about wire transfers or remittance transfers, please refer to Section 8 of this Agreement. 

5(b). Your Liability 

Your liability for an unauthorized EFT or a series of related unauthorized EFTs will be determined as follows:

Event: Loss or theft of Access Device (including username and password)

If you notify us...

Within two Business Days after learning of the loss or theft.

Your liability won't exceed...

Lesser of $50, OR the total amount of unauthorized EFTs that occur before notice to us.

Event: Loss or theft of Access Device (including username and password)

If you notify us...

More than two Business Days after learning of the loss or theft of your Access Device up to 60 days after we send you a statement showing the first unauthorized transfer made with Access Device.

Your liability won't exceed...

Lesser of $500, OR the sum of:

a) $50 or the total amount of unauthorized EFTs occurring in the first two Business Days whichever is less; AND

b) the amount of unauthorized EFTs occurring after two Business Days and before notice to us.

Event: Loss or theft of Access Device (including username and password)

If you notify us...

More than 60 days after we send you a statement showing first unauthorized EFT made with Access Device.

Your liability won't exceed...

  • For transfers occurring WITHIN the 60 day period: Lesser of $500, OR the sum of: (a) $50 or the total amount of unauthorized EFTs occurring in the first two Business Days whichever is less; AND (b) the amount of unauthorized EFTs occurring after two Business Days and before notice to us.
  • For transfers occurring AFTER the 60 day period, you may have unlimited liability, until you notify us.
Event: Unauthorized EFT(s) NOT involving loss or theft of an Access Device (including username and password)

If you notify us...

Within 60 days after we send you a statement on which the unauthorized transfer first appears.

Your liability won't exceed...

No liability.

Event: Unauthorized EFT(s) NOT involving loss or theft of an Access Device (including username and password)

If you notify us...

More than 60 days after we send you a statement on which the unauthorized transfer first appears.

Your liability won't exceed...

Unlimited liability for unauthorized EFTs occurring 60 days after the statement and before notice to us.

If your delay in notifying us was due to extenuating circumstances, we'll extend the times specified in the immediately preceding paragraphs to a reasonable period.

Note that these liability rules are established by Regulation E, which implements the federal Electronic Fund Transfer Act and do not apply to business accounts. Our agreements applicable to Wells Fargo debit and ATM cards may give you more liability protection for unauthorized debit and ATM card transactions, provided you report the transactions promptly. Please see the agreement you received with your debit or ATM card, and the Eligible Account agreement.

5(c). Errors/Unauthorized Electronic Fund Transfers/Questions

Here's how to notify us when you believe that an error, unauthorized EFT, or unauthorized transfer has been or may have been made:

  • Phone. 1-800-956-4442, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
  • Paper Mail. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., P.O. Box 6995, Portland, OR 97228-6995.

We may, from time to time, also permit notifications for certain errors to be submitted digitally through the Website. However, we offer these digital services as a convenience. If at any time this functionality is unavailable or you do not receive confirmation that any such dispute was submitted – whether as a result of technical errors or for any other reason – you must notify us of your dispute at either the phone number or mailing address listed immediately above.

To notify us of errors regarding EFTs on your applicable brokerage account, follow the procedures in your brokerage account agreement. To notify us of errors regarding EFTs on an account serviced by Trust Services, contact your account team.

To limit your liability for subsequent unauthorized transfers, or to report any other errors, we must hear from you no later than 60 days after the date we send the first statement on which the problem or error first appeared.

When contacting us about an error or with questions, please tell us:

  • Your name and account number (if any).
  • About the error or the transfer you question, and clearly explain why you believe it is an error or why you need more information.
  • To the extent possible, the dollar amount and date of the suspected error.

If you report a problem by phone, we may ask you to submit your complaint or question in writing within 10 Business Days. We'll determine whether an error occurred within 10 Business Days after we hear from you and will promptly correct any error. If we need more time to conduct our investigation, we’ll notify you of our need for an extension of up to 45 days. If we decide to do this, we'll provisionally credit your account within 10 Business Days for the amount you think is in error, so you can use the money during the time it takes us to complete our investigation. If we ask you to put your complaint or question in writing and don't receive it within 10 Business Days, we may not provisionally credit your account.

We may permit you to initiate or monitor the status of certain kinds of complaints or questions electronically on the Website. Complaints or questions you initiate via the process we provide on the Website will be considered as written notification.

For errors involving new accounts, point-of-sale, or foreign-initiated transactions, our investigation may take up to 90 calendar days. For new accounts, we may take up to 20 Business Days to credit your account for the amount you think is in error.

We will tell you the results within three Business Days after completing our investigation. If we decide that there was no error, or an error occurred that is different from the one you described, we will send you a written explanation and you can ask for copies of the documents that we used in our investigation.

5(d). Documentation

You have the right to find out whether an EFT was credited to or debited from your Eligible Account. To do so, contact us at the number listed on your statement for your Eligible Account.

We'll send you a monthly statement if there are EFTs in a particular month. Otherwise, we'll send you a statement at least quarterly.

You can get a receipt at the time you make any EFT to or from your account using one of our ATMs or when you use your card at a merchant terminal.

5(e). Handling Preauthorized (Recurring) Payments

Right to stop payment: If you have told us in advance to make regular (recurring) payments out of your account, you can stop any of these payments. Here's how: Call Wells Fargo Phone Bank at 1-800-869-3557, or write to us at Wells Fargo, Customer Correspondence, P.O. Box 6995, Portland, OR, 97228-6995, in time for us to receive your request three Business Days or more before the payment is scheduled to be made. If you call, we may also require you to put your request in writing and get it to us within 14 days after you call. Please refer to the account agreement governing your Eligible Account(s) for more information. To request a stop payment on a preauthorized EFT from an applicable brokerage account, follow the procedures noted in your brokerage account agreement.

Notice of varying amounts: If the amount of these regular (recurring) payments vary, the party you are going to pay should tell you 10 days before each payment, when it will be made and how much it will be. (The party you are going to pay may allow you to choose to get this notice only when the payment would differ by more than a certain amount from the previous payment, or when the amount would fall outside certain limits that you set.)

Liability for failure to stop payment: If you order us to stop one of these payments three Business Days or more before the transfer is scheduled, and we do not do so, we will pay for your losses or damages.

5(f). Our Liability for Failure to Make Transfers

Bill Pay is intended for your use only to pay bills, invoices, and requests for payment under Section 6(i) below, and not for any other purpose. Using Bill Pay to process payments on behalf of someone other than an owner is prohibited and will be grounds for termination of Bill Pay and your access to the Service.

We may use non-affiliated third parties acting on our behalf to process Bill Pay payments. These third-party processors must adhere to Wells Fargo's strict security and privacy-protection standards. Paper checks processed by non-affiliated third parties may show that they were drawn on the third-party processor, rather than on Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.

The date a Bill Pay payment starts processing is referred to in this Agreement as the "Payment Send On Date." Specific details about the Payment Send On Date will be provided on the Service Web pages when you schedule a Bill Pay payment. We may, at our option, pay or refuse to make bill payments funded by checking accounts, money market accounts, or a Brokerage Cash Services account if it would create an overdraft on those accounts. This decision remains discretionary regardless of whether we’ve previously honored or dishonored overdrafts.

If we receive a bill payment drawn against your checking account, money market, or a Brokerage Cash Services account, and there are insufficient available funds in that account to cover the payment, we may at our sole discretion:

  • Cover the payment by transferring available credit or funds from an account you have linked for Overdraft Protection, or
  • Pay the bill payment and create an overdraft on your account, or
  • Decline the bill payment, or
  • Re-attempt the bill payment the following Business Day (until this second attempt is completed, the payment is pending and cannot be canceled).

Any negative balance on your Funding Account will be governed by your applicable account agreements with us and fees may apply. 

If a Bill Pay Funding Eligible Account is an eligible line of credit or business credit card account, we may decline to make the payment unless that account has sufficient available credit to pay the bill on the Payment Send On Date. Your account's terms and conditions describe "over limit fees" that may apply to you if any bill payments, associated fees, or finance charges cause your credit account balance to exceed the credit limit. 

The dollar amount of bill payments through your credit account (whether we make these payments electronically or by check) will be charged to that credit account on the Payment Send On Date.

6(c). Stop/Change Payment

You have the right to stop or change any scheduled bill payment, if you: (1) do so within the Bill Pay secure online session or by calling Wells Fargo Online Customer Service at 1-800-956-4442, and (2) have submitted your request in time to provide us a reasonable opportunity to act on it before we pay, cash, or otherwise become obligated to pay your bill. See Bill Pay Payment Guarantee for further information.

Stop payment requests aren't guaranteed: for example, payees can present paper check payments to their bank before the stop payment has been properly processed, and once a paper check has been cashed by the payee or credited to the payee’s account it cannot be stopped. If we successfully stop the payment of a paper check, it may take up to seven Business Days for the funds to be credited back to your account.

6(d). Scheduling Payments

When making payments through Bill Pay, please allow enough time for your payee to receive your payment and credit your account properly. To avoid incurring a finance or other charge imposed by your payee, you must schedule a payment sufficiently in advance of the payment due date, so that the delivery date is before the payment due date.

Bill Pay payments sent by check will show the payer of the check as the "Name on Bill" you have provided for that payee record.

Payments must be scheduled before 7pm Pacific Time to be processed on that day. We will withdraw funds from your Bill Pay Funding Eligible Account on the Business Day following your Payment Send On Date (any applicable paper checks will reflect the date that funds are withdrawn). Your Available Balance may be reduced by the amount of your payment on the calendar day following your Payment Send On Date, if that day is not a Business Day. Payments scheduled from brokerage accounts, if permitted, or a Brokerage Cash Services account may have different cut-off times.

If a paper check is sent and the check is not presented for payment within 90 days, we'll stop payment on the check and credit the check amount back to your Bill Pay Funding Eligible Account.

To avoid sending duplicate Bill Pay payments, if you schedule more than one payment to the same payee for the same amount on the same date, only one payment will be sent.

In addition to the provisions in Section 5 above and in Section 17(c) below, please refer to our Bill Pay Payment Guarantee, which provides additional benefits in certain circumstances.

  • If you establish more than 999 payees.

  • For Eligible Accounts that are in default or subject to an automatic stay in bankruptcy.
  • Upon the death of an owner.

If Wells Fargo terminates your use of Bill Pay, your online bill payment information will be lost and all pending payments will be canceled and are your sole responsibility.

Once an eBill request is submitted, it may take up to ten (10) Business Days for a company to approve your eBill request. 8(a). Description

The Wells Fargo digital wire transfer service ("Wire Transfers") allows you to send money online to both personal and business accounts in the U.S. and in many countries. When you use Wire Transfers, you can instruct us to transfer funds by wire from your Eligible Account that you use to fund an online wire transfer ("Wires Funding Eligible Account"), with such instruction being an "Order". The following provisions supplement your applicable Wires Funding Eligible Account agreement. If there is any conflict between these provisions and your Wires Funding Eligible Account agreement, these provisions will control with respect to Wire Transfers.

You understand and agree that the provisions of Section 2(b) will apply to Wire Transfers.

8(b). Security Procedure

You agree that we will use the security procedure described in this section (“Security Procedure”) to verify the authenticity of an Order initiated on the Website from your Wires Funding Eligible Account. The Security Procedure consists of verifying your username and password, together with such other additional security and authentication methods as we may require from time to time, which may include device-based authentication (such as verification of a trusted device), application-based authentication (such as approval through the Wells Fargo mobile application), biometric authentication (such as facial recognition or other biometric identifiers), and code- or token-based authentication methods (such as one-time passcodes or random number generators). You agree that the Security Procedure is commercially reasonable. Wells Fargo employs the username and password standards set forth in Section 17(b), and you agree to protect your username and password pursuant to Section 17(d). Under Uniform Commercial Code Article 4A-202(b), the purpose of the Security Procedure is to verify the authenticity of an Order delivered to us in your name and not to detect errors in the transmission or content of an Order. An Order accepted by us in compliance with the Security Procedure will be effective as your Order for purposes of Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code. If you permit an AI Agent or other third party access to the Service, you acknowledge that doing so may adversely impact the commercially reasonable security procedures that you've otherwise agreed to, and you accept the risk of such access.

You agree to be bound by any Order that Wells Fargo receives and verifies following the Security Procedure, even if the Order was not authorized by you. You agree that we may be liable only for the minimum damages required to be paid under Uniform Commercial Code Article 4A. In no event will we be liable for any exemplary, special, indirect, or consequential loss, damage, costs, or expense of any nature, including lost profits, even if we have been informed of the possibility of such damages, except as may be required by law or regulation. In no event will Wells Fargo be liable for attorney’s fees. This Section 8(b) will control as the Security Procedure with respect to Orders for Wire Transfers instead of Section 17(c) below.

In addition to any applicable fees, Wells Fargo makes money when we convert one currency to another currency for you. The exchange rate used when Wells Fargo converts one currency to another is set at our sole discretion, and it includes a markup. The markup is designed to compensate us for several considerations including, without limitation, costs incurred, market risks, and our desired return. The applicable exchange rate does not include, and is separate from, any applicable fees. The exchange rate Wells Fargo provides to you may be different from exchange rates you see elsewhere. Different customers may receive different rates for transactions that are the same or similar. The applicable exchange rate may vary based on such factors including, but not limited to, currency pair, transaction size, payment channel, and product type, such as foreign currency cash, checks, remittances, and wire transfers. Foreign exchange markets are dynamic, and rates fluctuate over time based on market conditions, liquidity, and risks. Outside of regular market hours and during weekends, additional markups are added to the exchange rate to account for any exchange rate fluctuations. Wells Fargo is your arms-length counterparty on foreign exchange transactions. We may refuse to process any request for a foreign exchange transaction.

Incoming wire transfers received in a foreign currency for payment into your account will be converted into U.S. dollars using the applicable exchange rate without prior notice to you.

If your outgoing international wire transfer is returned to Wells Fargo, you may be credited back a lesser amount than the amount that was originally debited for your initial outgoing wire transfer. Fee(s) may be charged by Wells Fargo or other financial institutions (for instance, by beneficiary and intermediary banks) when a wire is returned. In addition, when a returned foreign currency wire is converted back to U.S. dollars, the U.S. dollar amount credited back to you may be less than the original amount we debited from your account due to fluctuation in the applicable exchange rate. You accept the risks of any unfavorable change in the applicable exchange rate. Wells Fargo will not be liable to you for a sum in excess of the amount that was originally debited for your initial outgoing wire transfer after it has been converted back to the original currency, even if there are favorable changes in the foreign exchange markets.

9(c). Types of Checks Eligible for the Mobile Deposit Service, and Other Requirements

You can deposit checks payable in U.S. dollars and drawn at any U.S. bank, including personal, business, and most government checks. Only checks, money orders, cashier's checks, or American Express traveler's checks, drawn on or payable at or through a U.S. bank, can be transmitted through the Mobile Deposit Service.

Checks must be payable to, and endorsed by, the account owner for the Eligible Account, as follows: before check photos are taken, the back of the check must be signed with "For Mobile Deposit at Wells Fargo Only" written below your signature (or if available, check the box that reads: "Check here if mobile deposit").

Checks and other items that are NOT eligible for the Mobile Deposit Service include: international checks, U.S. savings bonds, U.S. postal money orders, remotely created checks (whether in paper form or electronically created), electronically created items (items created electronically and not derived from a paper check), convenience checks (checks drawn against a line of credit), non-American Express traveler's checks, cash, checks that are illegible or contain MICR data that is not machine-readable, and duplicate checks.

After depositing your check using mobile deposit, you must:

  • Write "mobile deposit" and the date on the front of your check. The date should be the month, day, and year of your deposit; and
  • Securely store your check for 5 days after your deposit, and then destroy it. This allows sufficient time in case the original check is required for any reason.

You are prohibited from duplicate scanning, negotiating, and/or depositing the same original check, or substitute of that original check, using our Mobile Deposit Service or by any other means. Wells Fargo Digital Wires

Need your money to get there quickly and securely?

Use wire transfers to get funds to family, businesses, or internationally, where timing mattersOpens a modal dialog for footnote 1

The way to send money when faster is better

Around the globe

With Wells Fargo Digital Wires you can send money to both personal and business accounts in the U.S. and 200+ countries. Wells Fargo charges a $30 fee for digital wires and a $40 fee for branch wires. Other fees may apply. Fees may be waived if funded from an eligible Wells Fargo account type.

When timing is key

Domestic digital wires are typically sent the same business day if they are submitted by 3:00 pm Pacific Time. Otherwise, they will be sent the next business day. For international wires, depending on your recipient's country, delivery times may vary.

Convenience matters

With digital wires, you can:

  • Add a recipient once – we’ll save the details for next time
  • Set your language preference to Spanish

When currency counts

Send a wire:

  • In Foreign CurrenciesOpens a modal dialog for footnote 2
  • In U.S. dollars

View our Digital Wires supported countries (PDF)

Sign on to get started

Compare your options and fees

How to set up and send digital wires


  • Sign on to Wells Fargo Online .
  • Select Wire Money in the Transfer & Pay menu.
  • Add recipient details.
  • Send the wire (You must have a valid U.S. Mobile number or secure ID device to wire money).

Frequently asked questions

How do I send a digital wire?Opens a modal dialog for footnote 1 How do I send a digital wire?Opens a modal dialog for footnote 1
  • Sign on to Wells Fargo Online®, go to Transfer & Pay, and select Wire Money to get started.
  • Add your recipient, select funding account and amount (along with any additional details required for certain countries).
  • Review and send your payment.

You must have a current residence in the United States to send a Digital Wire. Customers living in U.S. territories (American Samoa, Guam, Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands) or other countries can’t send wires online.

How much money can I send and receive with Wells Fargo Digital Wires? How much money can I send and receive with Wells Fargo Digital Wires?

For your security, we limit the amount of money you can wire digitally. The amount you can send will vary based on your account and banking history, your recipient, and the transaction history of each recipient. We may adjust these limits at any time.

Your daily limit is the maximum you can send in a calendar day based on previous transactions and the recipient. Your rolling 30-day limit is the maximum you can send over a period of time going back 30 days.

To send a wire over your limit, visit a Wells Fargo branch.

Receiving limits
We don’t limit how much money you can receive with wires. However, the sender may be subject to limits on how much they can send you, based on the policies of their bank or credit union. 

What information do I need to wire money through Wells Fargo? What information do I need to wire money through Wells Fargo?

To send a wire, you will need:

  • Your recipient's name and address
  • The name of your recipient’s bank
  • A valid U.S. mobile number or RSA SecurID® device

To send a domestic wire, you will also need:

  • The routing (ABA/RTN) number for your recipient’s bank. If you don't know it, we'll help you find it on the Recipient's bank info screen.
  • Your recipient’s account number

To send an international wire, you will also need:

  • The SWIFT/BIC for your recipient’s bank. A SWIFT code or Bank Identification Code (BIC) identifies the bank that will receive your wire transfer. If you don’t know it, we'll help you find it on the Recipient's bank info screen.
  • Your recipient’s International Bank Account Number (IBAN). An IBAN identifies specific bank accounts at international banks. Depending on the country, we may ask you to provide an IBAN when you send an international wire transfer. If you don't know it, we'll help you find it on the Recipient's bank info screen.

Certain countries require additional codes as follows:

  • Australia: Australian Branch Code (BSB)
  • Canada: Canadian Payment Routing Number
  • Great Britain: U.K. Sort Code
  • India: IFSC Code
  • Mexico: CLABE
  • New Zealand, Cook Islands, Niue, Pitcairn and Tokelau: New Zealand Clearing Code
  • Some countries also require you to provide a purpose of payment

Wires FAQs

1.

Enrollment in Digital Wires is subject to eligibility requirements, and terms and conditions apply. Applicable outgoing or incoming wire transfer service fees apply, unless waived by the terms of your account. Your mobile carrier's message and data rates may apply. For more information, see the Wells Fargo Online Access Agreement and your applicable account fee disclosures for other terms, conditions, and limitations.

2.

Whether or not the wire transfer fee is waived, Wells Fargo makes money when we convert one currency to another currency for you. The exchange rate used when Wells Fargo converts one currency to another is set at our sole discretion, and it includes a markup. The markup is designed to compensate us for several considerations including, without limitation, costs incurred, market risks, and our desired return. The applicable exchange rate does not include, and is separate from, any applicable fees. The exchange rate Wells Fargo provides to you may be different from exchange rates you see elsewhere. Different customers may receive different rates for transactions that are the same or similar. The applicable exchange rate may vary based on such factors including, but not limited to, currency pair, transaction size, payment channel and product type, such as foreign currency cash, checks, remittances, and wire transfers. Foreign exchange markets are dynamic and rates fluctuate over time based on market conditions, liquidity, and risks. Outside of regular market hours and during weekends, additional markups are applied to the exchange rate to account for exchange rate fluctuations. Wells Fargo is your arms-length counterparty on foreign exchange transactions. We may refuse to process any request for a foreign exchange transaction.

Incoming wire transfers received in a foreign currency for payment into your account will be converted into U.S. dollars using the applicable exchange rate without prior notice to you. For more information, see the “Applicable Exchange Rate” and “Incoming international wire transfer” sections of the Deposit Account Agreement.

Fees may be charged by third parties or other banks, in addition to those described above.

/personal-loans/learn/different-types-of.html:
What are the different types of loans?

Published October, 2026    8 min read
In this article
  • How loans are categorized
  • Types of personal loans
  • High-cost loans to approach with caution
  • How to choose the right type of loan
  • Understanding loan types can narrow your search
Key takeaways
  • There are different types of loans to meet a variety of borrower needs, ranging from personal installment loans to short-term buy now, pay later agreements.
  • Loans can be divided into various categories or types according to their repayment structure, the type of interest charged, if it relies on collateral or not, and the intended use of the funds.
  • Understanding the various loan types before you shop around can help you pinpoint which categories of loans are best for your situation so you can narrow your search.

Anyone considering a loan will discover that there are many different types of personal loans available.

This guide breaks down the different loan types, identifies which types may be less consumer-friendly, and provides the foundation to help you decide which loan fits your situation.

How loans are categorized

Loans can be categorized at a high level based on several different criteria. Three high-level categories involve the type of underwriting used, the repayment structure, and the type of interest rate on the loan.

The first major category in which you can group loans is related to the type of underwriting criteria used: unsecured loans vs. secured or collateralized loans.

Another way to categorize loans involves the repayment structure. For instance, the loan can be either an installment loan that has a set term and an end date, or a revolving line of credit that can be used over and over.

Loans can also be broken into two different categories based on the type of interest rate: fixed or variable.

Here’s a closer look at these basic loan categories.

Secured vs. unsecured loans

Secured loans are backed by a collateral asset that provides “security” to the lender in case the borrower can’t pay back the loan. An example of a secured loan is an auto loan. If you don’t pay the monthly payment for the loan, the car can be repossessed.

Unsecured loans don’t use collateral, which is why they often have specific credit and income requirements.

Installment loans vs. revolving credit lines

Installment loans give the borrower a specific amount of time to repay the loan. Repayment typically occurs via fixed monthly payments throughout the term.

Revolving credit lines give borrowers a credit line that they can draw from whenever they wish, as long as there is available credit. Credit cards are an example of revolving credit.

Fixed-rate vs. variable-rate loans

Annual Percentage Rate (APR) is a major factor to consider when comparing loans. Most personal loans have fixed rates, meaning the same APR applies over the full term of the loan. But other loans can have variable rates, in which the APR fluctuates at various points in the term.

Types of personal loans

In addition to the high-level categories of loans, some loan types are based on what the loan is used for. For example, some personal loans are marketed as debt consolidation loans, medical loans, wedding loans, moving loans, or home improvement loans.

Other types of loans include co-signed and joint loans, which are for people who want to borrow with a co-borrower or who may not qualify on their own.

Additional types of loans may have a nontraditional payback structure, such as buy now, pay later loans or personal lines of credit.

Here are some of the different types of loans:

Unsecured personal loans

Unsecured personal loans are most common. Lenders evaluate applicants by looking at several factors, including credit history, income, and ability to repay. From there, the lender determines if the applicant meets their requirements and the loan rate for which they qualify.

Secured personal loans

Secured personal loans are collateralized, or backed by an asset. This removes some of the risk for the lender and, in some cases, allows borrowers who may not have strong credit to qualify.

Debt consolidation loans

Debt consolidation loans are a specific type of personal loan designed to pay off high-interest debt. Some lenders even send payments directly to creditors on your behalf. After old debts are paid, you are left with a single, fixed monthly payment.

Co-signed and joint loans

Cosigned loans allow someone with strong credit to serve as a backup for a person who has limited or weaker credit. The co-signer agrees to take on the loan payments if the primary borrower can’t meet their obligation, but the funds go to the primary borrower. Joint loans are for co-borrowers, meaning each party shares access to the loan funds as well as the responsibility to pay back the loan.

Personal lines of credit

Personal lines of credit are revolving credit lines. Borrowers can draw funds up to their approved credit limit. There is usually a minimum monthly payment due, but there’s no end date for when the line of credit must be fully repaid. In most cases, you can keep borrowing from the credit line as long as it stays open.

Buy now, pay later

Buy now, pay later (BNPL) is a popular type of short-term loan that splits a purchase into multiple payments. Depending on repayment terms, these types of loans may have no credit check, fees, or interest involved. However, it’s important to review terms because missing a BNPL payment or choosing a longer-term option could lead to additional costs.

Check my loan options

High-cost loans to approach with caution

When exploring different types of loans, you may find some lending products that aren’t consumer-friendly. These come with high fees, high rates, and strict repayment terms. They may make promises of “fast cash” and are often marketed to people who have poor credit and can’t qualify for traditional personal loans. Some of these products could qualify as predatory lending.

While considering such products, pay special attention to the terms and conditions to make sure you understand how the loan works. Choose a reputable lender that offers transparent terms and clarify anything you don’t understand.

If you need to rely on one of these loans in a pinch, consider establishing a plan for how you’ll repay it so that you don’t end up in a cycle of high-cost debt.

Payday loans

Payday loans are short-term loans (usually for $500 or less) with high fees. They typically offer fast funding, and you repay the lender directly from your next paycheck, either with a post-dated check or via electronic access to your checking account. Payday loans are illegal in some states.

Title loans

A title loan is a secured loan that uses your vehicle title as collateral. This is often a short-term, high-interest loan. The lender places a lien on your car until you repay the loan, and if you can’t make payments, they can legally repossess your vehicle.

Cash advances

A cash advance is another type of short-term loan that comes with higher costs. A credit card cash advance allows you to draw funds from your credit limit. There’s typically a fee and a separate, higher APR associated with that balance. There are also paycheck cash advance apps that allow you to access your paycheck early, though fees or other charges may apply.

Pawnshop loans

A pawnshop loan is when you use a personal item of value as collateral to borrow cash. The pawnshop determines how much to lend you (usually offering an amount significantly lower than the item’s value). Then, the shop holds on to your item until you repay the loan, plus interest and fees. If you fail to repay, the pawnshop keeps the item.

How to choose the right type of loan

To choose the right type of loan, figure out how much you need to borrow, the strength of your credit history, and a repayment plan that fits your budget. Ideally, you would borrow exactly the amount you need, have ample time to repay, and do so at the lowest possible additional cost.

Some personal loans are designed for borrowers who need higher amounts and want to pay them back over several years, while others provide smaller amounts to get you through a short-term cash flow challenge. Higher amounts usually mean going for a personal loan or line of credit. Typically consumers who need a few hundred dollars will choose a BNPL pay or some type of cash advance.

Credit status also plays a role in determining which type of loan is best. Stronger credit and steady income will unlock more options and improve your chances of qualifying for a competitive interest rate. People with low or limited credit may consider co-signed loans or secured loans.

The last step is figuring out how much you can reasonably afford to pay back and when. Longer loans may offer a lower monthly payment, but you will pay more in interest over the life of the loan. For smaller loans that require repayment within a few weeks, make sure you can handle paying back that amount in a shorter timeframe.

Understanding loan types can narrow your search

Understanding the different types of personal loans is the first step in finding the best option for your situation. The next step is choosing a lender. Even among the same loan type, a lender’s offers and terms can vary widely. Once you know your ideal loan type, compare rates and terms to find the best plan for you.

FAQs about the different types of personal loans

What are the most common types of loans? What are the most common types of loans?

The most common types of loans are installment loans with fixed monthly payments. Borrowers have a specific amount of time to complete payment.

What's the difference between a secured and unsecured loan? What's the difference between a secured and unsecured loan?

A secured loan is backed by collateral, meaning that if you don’t pay, the lender can take possession of your asset (such as a car or home). An unsecured loan does not use collateral. To qualify, you must meet the lender’s credit and income requirements for borrowing.

What is the most common type of personal loan? What is the most common type of personal loan?

The most common type of personal loan is an unsecured loan. Most personal loans require credit underwriting to determine if the borrower qualifies, rather than using assets as collateral.

Which type of loan is the most straightforward to get approved for? Which type of loan is the most straightforward to get approved for?

Loans that don’t require a credit check or loans secured by some type of collateral usually have a more simplified approval process. Loans without a credit check may be more costly because they’re usually aimed at borrowers who don’t have strong credit scores. Secured loans backed by an asset give the lender some recourse if you are unable to pay, so they sometimes have less stringent approval requirements.

What are some loan red flags to be aware of? What are some loan red flags to be aware of?

Some loans may have high upfront costs or difficult repayment terms. Loans with many fees or very high APR can make it difficult for borrowers already facing financial strain.

How do I choose the right loan for my needs? How do I choose the right loan for my needs?

Choosing the right loan first requires self-assessment to see what types of loans you may qualify for and if you may need a co-signer. From there, think about the loan amount you need, how much monthly payment you can afford, and what your ideal repayment timeline would look like.

Are all personal loans installment loans? Are all personal loans installment loans?

Personal loans will typically be installment loans. That means you will receive a lump sum from the lender that you’ll pay back in equal monthly payments over the course of the loan term.

Roof financing: How to finance a new roof

Published October, 2026    6 min read
In this article
  • Can you finance a roof?
  • How much does a new roof cost?
  • Check your insurance before you finance
  • Roof financing options
  • How to finance a new roof
  • How to choose the right roof financing option
Key takeaways
  • If your home needs a new roof, it can cost several thousand dollars or more depending on the size and type of home. 
  • There are several roof financing options, including taking a personal loan, tapping into home equity, or working with the contractor on a payment plan. 
  • Before seeking financing for a new roof, check with your homeowners insurance company to see if you are eligible for a partial or full payment.

Putting a new roof on your home can be an expensive but necessary undertaking. In many cases, homeowners must turn to roof financing to help them cover the cost. 

To help you decide which type of roof financing makes sense for you, learn more about the unique benefits and drawbacks of the various types of financing, and why it’s always wise to check your homeowners insurance first.

Can you finance a roof?

Yes, you can finance a roof. As a major home improvement expense, many people may not have enough cash reserves on hand to cover such a high cost. As such, there are multiple lending products homeowners can rely on to help pay for a new roof or roof repair.

How much does a new roof cost? 

The average cost of a professional roof replacement is about $10,000, but the price can have a much wider range depending on the roof size, type of roofing material used, the pitch of the roof, and where the home is located. Industry estimates say new roof costs can range from a starting cost of $6,000 to as high as $45,000.

Check your insurance before you finance

If you need a new roof due to sudden storm, wind, or hail damage, check your homeowners insurance policy before committing to out-of-pocket financing. In many cases, policies provide partial or full coverage for roof repairs or total replacement resulting from covered perils. Contact your insurance carrier as soon as damage occurs to file a claim; while you should take immediate temporary measures to prevent water damage (such as tarping exposed sections), hold off on permanent replacement work until an adjuster inspects the property.

Roof financing options 

If homeowners insurance will not cover the cost of the roof, homeowners have a few different lending products they can use to help finance a new roof. The amount needed, the borrower’s credit status, and how much equity is available to tap into can help determine the right type of roof financing for you. Also be sure to review full terms and conditions when making your final decision.

Personal loans 

A personal loan can be used to pay for a new roof if you’re looking for an unsecured product that does not use your home as collateral. This type of installment loan usually has a fixed interest rate, a straightforward application process, and fast funding. Borrowers may also have a range of loan terms from which to choose, giving them some control over how much they will pay monthly.

Home equity loans and HELOCs 

Home improvement projects, such as replacing a roof, are among the most common reasons homeowners tap into their home equity through a fixed-rate home equity loan or a revolving home equity line of credit (HELOC). One potential advantage is tax deductibility: if you use the borrowed funds to substantially improve your home and itemize your return, the interest paid may be tax-deductible (consult a qualified tax advisor regarding your eligibility). Drawbacks include closing costs, a longer appraisal and underwriting process, and the requirement to pledge your home as collateral.

Cash-out refinance 

Another way to use your home equity to fund a new roof is to take a cash-out refinance. This is when you refinance your existing mortgage into a new home loan, but increase the loan size so that there is some excess cash for you to use. This option can be worth exploring if you were thinking of refinancing anyway, and if you can qualify for a lower interest rate than your current mortgage.

Roofing company or contractor financing 

If you prefer to work out a payment plan directly with the roofing company or contractor, many roofing contractors offer direct financing programs or partnerships with third-party lenders.

Government-insured loans 

The Federal Housing Administration (FHA), an agency within HUD, insures private lenders through programs like the Title I Property Improvement Loan program to help homeowners finance essential repairs and replacements. Not all projects will qualify, as there are specific eligibility criteria such as income level, property type, and location.

Get the funds you need with a personal loan

Check your rate and explore loan options with no impact to your credit score.

Check my loan options

How to finance a new roof 

Here are some steps to take if you want to finance a new roof. 

  1. Decide how much you need to borrow. Before you choose a type of financing, you should get a couple of estimates so you know how much the roof will cost. If it’s on the less expensive side, you may decide to use a personal loan over a home equity loan, for example. 
  2. Check your credit status and home equity (if applicable). Most lenders will review your credit score and other factors to determine if you are eligible for financing and to calculate your interest rate. Check your score in advance. If you’re considering a home equity loan or HELOC, verify how much equity you have in the home to see if those programs are feasible. 
  3. Choose your financing option and compare lenders. Based on your funding needs and financial situation, choose your financing type and get some lender quotes to compare rates and terms. 
  4. Apply for financing. Once you choose the best lender offer, begin your application. Note that personal loans and contractor financing may offer a faster application process compared to home equity products. 
  5. Have a repayment plan. Before you accept an approved financing offer, make sure you understand the terms and are able to meet your repayment obligations. Once you accept the loan or credit offer, consider automating your monthly payments so you stick with your repayment schedule.

How to choose the right roof financing option 

Choosing the right new roof financing or roof replacement financing option comes down to asking yourself questions like these. 

  • How much financing do you need? There’s a big difference between needing $5,000 versus $40,000. Knowing how much you need to borrow can influence your financing decision. 
  • What type of financing can you qualify for? Do you have a high percentage of home equity and excellent credit? If so, that may point you toward a HELOC or home equity loan. If your credit isn’t as strong, you may consider working with the contractor on a payment plan. Will homeowners insurance pay for a new roof? Will homeowners insurance pay for a new roof?

Homeowners insurance may pay for a new roof in some circumstances. For example, if you’re replacing a roof that was damaged by wind or hail, your policy may cover it. Before you replace your roof, it’s always wise to speak with your insurance carrier to see if there is any coverage available.

Personal loans offer simple applications, fast funding, and a fixed installment payment for a specified loan term. Home equity loans involve a more detailed application and have closing costs, but you have a longer timeframe to make the repayment and may offer tax-deductible interest if used for substantial home improvements (consult a tax advisor regarding eligibility). Anytime you apply for a new loan or line of credit, such as roof financing, it can generate a hard credit inquiry when the lender pulls your credit report. This may cause a temporary score drop. Opening a new credit line or loan will also alter different aspects of your credit file, including your overall amount of outstanding debt, the average age of your credit, and your credit mix (the types of credit lines you are managing). Ultimately, if you responsibly manage your roof financing with consistent, on-time payments, that positive activity can support a healthy credit profile over time.

How to get a $5,000 loan

Published October, 2026    7 min read

In this article

  • Where can you get a $5,000 loan?
  • How much does a $5,000 loan cost per month?
  • What you need to qualify for a $5,000 loan

  • Should you get a $5,000 loan?
Key takeaways
  • If you’re looking for a $5,000 loan, you may first want to check your credit and compare offers from banks, credit unions, and online lenders. 
  • To qualify for a $5,000 loan, most lenders will review your credit history and verify your income to make sure you can repay the loan. The best offers often go to people with strong credit. 
  • To decide if a $5,000 loan is right for you, consider researching what your monthly payment will be and how it will impact your budget.

If you find yourself in need of money to help cover an unexpected expense, fund a home repair, or reduce high-interest debt, you may be wondering if a $5,000 loan is right for you. 

Many lenders provide $5,000 personal loans with funding available within a few days or less. Here’s what you need to know about how to qualify, what the monthly repayment will be, and alternative finance options.

How to get a $5,000 loan

If you’re interested in getting a $5,000 loan, you can find a lender and apply in a few steps. 

  1. Do a self-assessment. Most lenders have eligibility requirements that include a minimum credit score. Before you begin shopping for a loan, it’s a good idea to pull your free credit reports and credit score to see where you stand. The stronger your credit is, the more likely you are to have multiple lenders competing for your business with favorable rates. 
  2. Compare lenders. Consider researching lenders or services that allow you to prequalify and see rate quotes without impacting your credit. This can give you a good sense of the rate range you may qualify for before you move forward with a full application. Getting a few quotes also lets you compare lender offers head to head to narrow down your options. Compare factors like Annual Percentage Rate (APR), fees, opportunities for rate discounts, and other loan terms. 
  3. Go over your numbers one more time. You want to make sure the loan’s monthly payment will work for your budget. Also look at the total cost of borrowing (which includes all interest and fees) to make sure you are comfortable with the loan offer. 
  4. Submit the loan application. See what documents the lender requires and gather them so that you have them ready. If you’re applying online, you can take photos or scan your documents for upload. Some lenders may have you apply over the phone with a loan specialist guiding you through the application. Or, you could apply in person at a bank branch or loan office, in which case, you can bring the required paperwork with you.

Where can you get a $5,000 loan? 

To get a $5,000 personal loan, most borrowers go through a bank, credit union, or online lender. 

Traditional banks and credit unions: Most banks and credit unions offer personal loans, so if you have an existing relationship with one, those institutions may be a good place to start. If you already bank with the lender, some of your information may already be on file. Certain banks and credit unions may also offer special terms or rate discounts for customers, such as a lower APR if you make automatic payments from your checking account. 

Online lenders: There are a number of online lending companies that offer $5,000 personal loans. The appeal of this option is being able to complete the process online. Some online lenders advertise rapid decisions or funding, though they may also require a degree of comfort with technology or smart devices. There is also often no physical location to visit for people who prefer in-person support. Additionally, consider researching any online lender to ensure it’s a legitimate and reputable company.

How much does a $5,000 loan cost per month?

Your monthly cost for a $5,000 loan mostly depends on the loan term and the APR. Always refer to your loan’s terms and conditions for full details. 

The loan term is the length of the loan. If you choose a longer term, you will typically make lower monthly payments. However, you’ll also pay more over the life of the loan because of the additional interest that will accrue. 

The second major factor impacting your monthly loan cost is the APR. A $5,000 loan’s interest rate depends on your creditworthiness and the lender. A lower rate means a lower monthly payment. 

Here are several examples of what a monthly payment on a $5,000 loan could look like. They all assume a fixed APR, equal monthly payments, and no additional fees.

This is important since you want to make sure your budget can handle any new monthly payment you take on. If a monthly payment seems too high for you, you may want to review longer-term loans. Or, if you think you can handle a shorter term, a slightly higher monthly payment can help reduce your overall borrowing cost.

What you need to qualify for a $5,000 loan 

Eligibility requirements for a $5,000 loan depend on the lender. If you’re applying for an unsecured personal loan, meaning there is no collateral to back up your loan, lenders will likely evaluate how risky it is to lend to you. In other words, they will look at your credit history and credit score, as well as make sure you have the capacity to pay back the loan. 

Creditworthiness: Many personal loan lenders will have a minimum credit score requirement. The actual number varies. Borrowers with stronger credit profiles generally qualify for lower rates. Some specialized lenders offer loans to people with limited credit or poor credit, though costs may be higher. 

Income: Lenders will want to verify that you have reliable income and/or are employed to qualify for a loan. This is why they usually ask for documentation like pay stubs, W-2 forms, or bank statements. Some lenders have a minimum annual income threshold requirement, while others may consider applications on a case-by-case basis. 

Lenders may also have lawful eligibility requirements.

Alternatives to a $5,000 loan 

If you decide that you don’t want a $5,000 loan, there are alternate funding sources. These may include: 

Credit cards: If you have a large purchase to make, you could see if you qualify for a credit card that has a 0% introductory APR offer. This can give you a set period of time to pay down the purchase with no additional interest. Once that period ends, the card’s specific terms will apply. 

Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL): BNPL allows you to split up the cost of a purchase into a few equal payments, but there may be late fees and other costs. This option also usually doesn’t require a credit check, but every provider is different. You may have to pay off the purchase in a shorter period of time compared to a personal loan. 

Line of credit: This type of product is more flexible (like a credit card) in that you can borrow what you need, make payments, and draw from the credit line over and over. Qualifying for a line of credit usually involves eligibility requirements similar to those for a personal loan.

Should you get a $5,000 loan? 

Deciding if you should get a $5,000 loan is a personal decision. First, it’s important to weigh the full cost of the loan and make sure you will be able to fulfill the monthly repayment obligation. You may also want to consider if a personal loan will create more financial stress or make it difficult to maintain your credit. 

Next, think about why you’re seeking the loan. Is the reason worth taking on a monthly bill for the next several years? Is it something you can delay so you can save up to pay for it upfront? Do you have access to other funding sources? 

Thinking through these questions can help you make a more informed borrowing decision.

How to lower your personal loan rate and total cost

Published October, 2026    6 min read
In this article
  • What makes up your total loan cost?
  • Improve your credit score to get a lower rate
  • Compare lenders and prequalify
  • Refinance your personal loan to a lower rate
  • Make extra payments toward the principal
  • Choose a shorter loan term
  • Enroll in autopay and pay on time
  • When you can't lower your rate
Key takeaways
  • Personal loans can help give you access to a lump sum of funding, but there is a borrowing cost involved.
  • Finding and qualifying for a more favorable personal loan rate is one way to lower the cost of your loan.
  • Some ways to reduce your loan rate or cost include improving your credit, refinancing, comparing lenders, and making additional payments to shorten your loan term and pay less interest.

If you are in the market for a personal loan, you may be wondering: how can you reduce your total loan cost? You’ve probably heard that getting a lower rate offer is one way to minimize your borrowing costs. There are a few things you can do to lower your personal loan rate or pay less over the life of the loan.

Learn how strategies such as improving your credit, comparing lenders, and refinancing can affect your loan costs.

What makes up your total loan cost?

Total loan cost is made up of the principal, interest, and any additional fees. Here’s a more in-depth look at the main components of your total loan cost.

  • Principal: This is the sum of money you borrow, or the total funding amount that the lender deposits into your account.
  • Interest: This is the cost of borrowing, or the amount charged to you by the lender. Personal loans typically have fixed interest rates that remain the same over the life of the loan.
  • Fees: Some lenders charge fees to borrowers, including origination fees, application fees, or penalty fees (such as for late or missed payments).

The annual percentage rate (APR) reflects the annual cost of borrowing and may include certain fees in addition to interest.

The other important factor that impacts loan cost is the loan term, or the length of the loan. The longer the loan term, the higher your total loan cost will be because you will be paying interest for a longer period of time.

Improve your credit score to get a lower rate

Lenders typically have an interest rate range for their products, with rates generally varying based on an applicant’s creditworthiness and other factors. Credit scores are one factor lenders may use to assess an applicant’s creditworthiness.

Credit scores can be affected by factors such as payment history, amounts owed, length of credit history, credit mix, and recent credit activity.

If you’re thinking of applying for a personal loan, tracking and understanding your credit score and improving your credit may help strengthen your application and could help you qualify for more competitive terms. Check your credit reports and correct any errors, continue paying bills on time, and work to reduce your outstanding credit card balances.

Compare lenders and prequalify

Another way to lower your personal loan cost is by shopping around to compare loan offers. Some borrowers skip this step and accept the first loan offer they receive, and they could be missing out on lower-cost loan options.

Many lenders allow you to explore personal loan offers or request quotes online. Some lenders offer prequalification using a soft credit inquiry, which generally does not affect your credit score.

Once you have a few loan comparisons in front of you, you can decide which one may best fit your needs.

Refinance your personal loan to a lower rate

Refinancing may be worth considering if you can qualify for more favorable loan terms. If you are able to qualify for a lower rate via a refinance, you may be able to lower your monthly payment and/or reduce the overall cost of your loan. For example, if you took a personal loan a couple of years ago when your credit wasn’t strong but now your score has improved, you might be able to find a lower rate by refinancing.

Compare the costs of refinancing with the potential savings to determine if refinancing makes financial sense for you. For example, if the interest rate drop isn’t significant enough to offset any fees, it may not be worth pursuing. Also, if refinancing extends the loan term, your monthly payment could decrease, though you may end up increasing your total loan cost.

Make extra payments toward the principal

The big question that most borrowers have is: How can you reduce total loan cost? One way is to pay down the loan faster by making extra principal payments. Here are a couple of reasons additional principal payments may reduce your borrowing costs.

  1. For loans where interest accrues based on the outstanding principal balance, reducing that balance faster may reduce the total interest you pay.
  2. Shortening your loan term by paying it off earlier means you may pay less interest overall.

First, check with your lender to understand how extra payments are applied to your loan balance. Second, confirm that your lender does not charge a prepayment penalty.

Choose a shorter loan term

If you’re trying to keep your overall borrowing costs lower, then consider choosing a shorter loan term. The longer your loan term, the longer you’ll pay interest, which can increase your total borrowing costs.

However, you also need to balance potential savings against choosing a monthly payment you can comfortably afford. Longer terms are sometimes attractive because they reduce the minimum monthly payment required, which can mean less strain on your budget. Choose a term with a monthly payment that fits comfortably within your budget, including room for unexpected expenses.

Enroll in autopay and pay on time

When you take out a personal loan, enrolling in autopay may have several benefits. For example, some lenders offer an interest-rate discount for enrolling in autopay.

Autopay may also help reduce the risk of accidentally missing a payment, provided sufficient funds are available in the linked account. This can help you avoid late fees (if applicable) and potential negative effects on your credit history or score.

When you can't lower your rate

When comparing personal loans, consider the interest rate alongside fees, repayment terms, monthly payments, and total borrowing costs. In some situations, there may be limited opportunities to lower your personal loan rate. These can include:

  • You were already offered the lender’s lowest available rate. If you qualify for the lender’s lowest available rate and have already used any available rate discounts, there may be limited opportunities to reduce your rate further.
  • You don’t have time to make significant credit improvements. Changes to your credit profile can take time, and improving your credit doesn’t guarantee a lower loan rate.

If you are not able to get a lower personal loan rate, there are still strategies you can use to reduce your borrowing cost. For example, making additional payments when your budget allows may help you save on interest overall.
