/personal-loans/learn/pay-off-personal-l.html:
Paying off a personal loan early: What you need to know

Published October, 2026    6 min read
In this article
  • What is a prepayment penalty?
  • Can you pay off a personal loan early?
  • Pros of paying off a personal loan early
  • Cons of paying off a personal loan early
  • Does paying off a loan early hurt your credit?
  • How to pay off a personal loan early
  • How to calculate your early payoff savings
  • Should you pay off your personal loan early?
Key takeaways
  • Personal loans have an end date, but borrowers have the option to pay the loan off early. 
  • Potential drawbacks include early payoff fees with some lenders and reduced budget flexibility for emergencies. 
  • If you can pay off a personal loan early, you may save money in interest charges and use the budgeted amount to focus on other financial goals.

Paying off a personal loan early may sound ideal. You’ll have one less debt to worry about, and you could allocate those funds toward another debt. However, it’s not that simple, and paying off a loan early may have consequences. 

Learn more about some of the potential advantages and disadvantages to paying a loan off early.

What is a prepayment penalty?

A prepayment penalty on a personal loan is a fee charged when borrowers complete the loan payoff before the agreed-upon end of the repayment term. Wells Fargo personal loans have no origination fees or prepayment penaltiesOpens a modal dialog for footnote 1, meaning you can pay off your balance early at any time without incurring extra fees. If your loan is with another lender, check your original loan agreement or contact customer service to verify whether early-payoff fees apply.

Can you pay off a personal loan early? 

In most cases, you can pay off a personal loan early. However, some lenders charge a prepayment penalty, or they may have a required time period for you to carry the loan before you can pay off the balance. 

It’s important to check the loan terms to confirm if there’s a prepayment fee. If there is, you can check to see how it compares to what you could save in interest by paying early.

Pros of paying off a personal loan early 

Paying off a personal loan early can help you save money because you’ll pay less interest and free up some cash flow. The key is to find the right balance where these payments do not cause financial stress in other areas of your budget.

Save money on interest 

The biggest advantage of paying off a loan early is that you pay less interest. On simple interest loans, interest is charged each month on the remaining principal balance. If you accelerate your payoff by paying more each month, it will reduce both the total months in repayment and the total amount of interest charged.

One less bill to worry about 

When budgets are tight, eliminating a fixed monthly bill can provide relief and flexibility. It can also give you a psychological win to know that you successfully paid off an installment loan, and did it early.

More cash flow to work with 

Once your personal loan is paid in full, consider redirecting those former monthly payments toward other financial priorities. Some options include increasing your emergency fund and retirement savings contributions.

Cons of paying off a personal loan early 

Paying off a personal loan early sounds like a positive thing, but there may be consequences.

Putting strain on your budget 

If you spend too much on paying down the loan early, you could put yourself in a risky position. This may cause you to rely on credit cards or other types of borrowing in the case of an emergency expense.

Not focusing on more impactful debt 

Some debt costs more than others. If you carry balances on credit cards, for example, you may pay a higher Annual Percentage Rate (APR) on the credit card debt than on a personal loan. In those situations, it may make more financial sense to pay down the higher-interest debts first.

Potential fees 

Some personal loans have prepayment penalties. If you plan to pay your loan off early, check the terms and conditions to see if they include any early payment fees.

Get the funds you need with a personal loan

Check your rate and explore loan options with no impact to your credit score.

Check my loan options

Does paying off a loan early hurt your credit? 

A personal loan is a type of credit product, so it is factored into your credit score. You may see score fluctuations when you apply for and open the loan, during the repayment phase, and when you pay off the balance. 

Paying off a loan early could result in a temporary, small drop in credit score since it changes your “credit mix,” which is one of the factors considered by credit scoring algorithms. Credit scores look favorably at customers who manage different types of credit, including revolving lines like credit cards and installment loans like personal loans. If you complete a loan payoff and no longer have an installment product open, you may see that reflected in your credit score. 

On the other hand, if you make on-time payments throughout your loan term, you may see an incremental, positive change to your credit score. Additionally, paying down loan balances reduces your debt-to-income (DTI) ratio, the percentage of your gross monthly income dedicated to debt payments. While DTI does not directly affect credit scores, a lower DTI ratio improves your overall financial standing and may help you qualify for future borrowing, such as a mortgage or auto loan.

How to pay off a personal loan early 

Paying off a loan early means your balance is zeroed out before the loan’s official end date. Here are some ways to close out the balance and potentially save money on interest. 

  • Pay more than the minimum amount due. With an installment loan, you have a fixed payment throughout the loan term that you must pay each month. Let’s say you have to pay $250 per month for 24 months. If you increase your monthly payment to $325 per month, you will pay the loan off sooner and with reduced interest charges. 
  • Make extra payments. If you have extra room in your budget, you could make additional payments on your personal loan. Remember to indicate to the financial institution that you want to use the extra payment toward the principal. You may need to speak with customer service to do this. 
  • Make a lump sum payment before the end of the loan term. If you happen to come into a large sum of money and decide you want to pay off your personal loan, start by asking the lender for the “payoff amount.” The amount fluctuates each day due to daily interest. Once you know the exact amount, you can submit the payment. 

If you’re aiming to pay off a personal loan early, the key is to find a happy medium where you can pay more than the minimum amount due on your personal loan but not so much that you have no margin of error left in your budget.

How to calculate your early payoff savings 

One deciding factor for paying off your personal loan early is to see how much it could save you. There are calculators online that can show you how various payment amounts and timelines can impact your overall loan cost. 

You can also do the math on your own by taking the total interest paid under your original loan schedule and subtracting the total interest you would pay under an accelerated payment plan. If there are any prepayment fees, subtract them from the interest savings.

Should you pay off your personal loan early? 

Whether you should pay your personal loan off early depends on your financial situation. If you make bigger loan payments to remove a few months from your loan term, it may be a positive for your finances. However, making large payments that stretch your budget to its limits or deplete your savings could leave you with less of a financial cushion. 

Other factors to weigh include the early prepayment penalty and whether you have other debt with high interest that could be worth paying down first.

FAQs about paying off a personal loan early

Do you still owe interest if you pay off a personal loan early? Do you still owe interest if you pay off a personal loan early?

Interest stops accruing when the principal balance is paid in full. You can avoid lingering daily interest charges by learning the total payoff amount for the loan on the specific day you want to make the payment.

Is it better to pay off a personal loan early or build savings first? Is it better to pay off a personal loan early or build savings first?

If you have the choice between paying off a personal loan early and building savings, you may want to put a specific amount of money aside for emergencies before making aggressive debt payments. Once you reach the emergency fund total, you could repurpose extra funds toward your loan balance and your savings at the time.

How do I find my exact loan payoff amount? How do I find my exact loan payoff amount?

You can usually find your exact loan payoff amount by logging into your account. You can also contact your lender directly to ask for your payoff amount. This is an important step when you want to pay your loan off early because the payoff amount changes every day due to interest.

Does paying extra always go toward the principal? Does paying extra always go toward the principal?

Extra personal loan payments may not automatically go toward the principal. You may have to check a box on the bank’s app or website to indicate your payment preference. If you don’t specify how to apply your payment, it may be recorded as a prepayment for future months.

How long does it take for your credit score to recover after early payoff? How long does it take for your credit score to recover after early payoff?

A small credit score drop after paying off a personal loan early is often temporary. How much and how quickly your credit score recovers will depend on your broader credit profile, including your payment history and remaining credit utilization.

Emergency loans: What they are and how to get one

Published October, 2026    7 min read
In this article
  • What is an emergency loan?
  • How to get an emergency loan
  • Where can I get an emergency loan?
  • Types of emergency loans
  • What can you use an emergency loan for?
  • Alternatives to emergency loans
Key takeaways
  • Emergency loans are unsecured personal loans that are used to cover unexpected expenses. 
  • Many lenders offer fast funding, often within a few business days or hours, though borrowers should exercise caution with high-cost options like payday and title loans. 
  • Alternatives for covering urgent expenses include existing emergency savings, credit cards, or borrowing against home equity, each with distinct costs and risks.

For times when an unexpected expense arises, many people use emergency loans as a financial lifeline to help cover the cost. These loans can often provide fast funding and allow the borrower to pay off the balance in smaller chunks over a period of time. However, when considering emergency loans, it’s important to work with a legitimate lender and avoid predatory products that have unfavorable fees and terms. 

Here’s what you need to know about emergency loans.

What is an emergency loan? 

An emergency loan is an unsecured personal loan used primarily to cover an unexpected expense. Borrowers often turn to personal loans for unplanned costs such as major home or auto repairs, out-of-pocket medical bills, or urgent travel to assist a family member. Emergency personal loans allow borrowers to divide the total expense plus interest into fixed, predictable monthly payments over a predetermined term.

How to get an emergency loan 

Getting an emergency personal loan involves a straightforward application process. Because these loans are typically unsecured (requiring no collateral), lenders evaluate your credit history, debt-to-income ratio, and income to determine eligibility and your specific interest rate. 

Start by analyzing your financial situation: 

  • Review your credit score: Most lenders offer their most competitive rates to borrowers with higher credit scores, though options may be available for fair credit profiles. 
  • Evaluate your budget: Determining what you can comfortably afford each month helps identify your target loan term. Longer-term loans lower your monthly payment, but they typically result in paying more total interest over the life of the loan. 
  • Determine your borrowing need: Lenders may approve you for more than you request, but borrowing only what is necessary helps keep monthly payments manageable. 

Shop and compare terms: 

  • Check your rate: Many lenders, including Wells Fargo, offer rate-checking tools that allow you to check potential rates with a soft credit check that won't impact your credit score. 
  • Review all terms: Compare annual percentage rates (APRs), origination fees, repayment schedules, and lender reputations. 

Once you choose your lender, you can begin the application process. In some cases, this is done entirely online, while some emergency personal loan lenders allow you to apply over the phone or in person at a branch. 

  • Get your documentation ready. You may be asked to share documents to prove your identity and verify your income and employment, such as a state ID, pay stubs, and bank statements. 
  • Receive an official loan offer. Once your application is processed, the lender will alert you if you’ve been approved. If so, and you choose to accept and sign the loan offer, you will receive funds shortly thereafter. This process can take anywhere from a few hours to several days depending on the lender and loan details. 
  • Begin repayment. If you have the option to set up automatic payments, that is an easy way to ensure that you don’t miss any due dates.

Where can I get an emergency loan? 

Emergency loans, or personal loans, are available from banks, credit unions, and online lenders. Other private lenders may offer different types of emergency loan products, but those often charge disproportionately high fees and interest rates that can trap borrowers in a cycle of debt. If possible, consider working with a reputable lender to avoid high-cost, high-risk lending products.

Banks and credit unions 

Banks and credit unions can be a good place to begin your emergency loan search. These financial institutions are well-regulated and offer dedicated customer support, often including in-person assistance at local branch locations. Additionally, having an established relationship with a bank or credit union may help expedite your application process or qualify you for relationship discounts and preferred terms.

Online lenders 

There are many reputable online lenders that offer emergency loans. This option may be well suited if you prefer a mostly digital experience, and in some cases, online lenders can offer faster processing and funding.

Lenders to avoid (payday and title lenders)

Borrowers who have difficulty qualifying for a personal loan through a bank or reputable online lender may consider payday or auto title loans. However, these products often carry exceptionally high APRs and short repayment windows. Some require direct debit access to your bank account, which can strain cash flow and contribute to a recurring cycle of debt.

Get the funds you need with a personal loan

Check your rate and explore loan options with no impact to your credit score.

Check my loan options

Types of emergency loans 

Different financing products can help manage an emergency expense, including unsecured personal loans, secured options, and revolving lines of credit.

Personal loans 

An emergency loan is typically a fixed-rate personal loan. Borrowers receive a lump sum and repay it in fixed monthly installments over a set period. This provides the borrower with predictable payments and often lower interest rates than standard credit cards.

Credit card cash advances 

Credit card cash advances are a type of short-term cash loan that you borrow from your card’s credit line. The amount is added to your total balance owed, the same way that a purchase would be. But the difference is you’ll usually also be charged a fee, and the amount of cash borrowed will incur a separate, usually higher, APR.

Home equity loans and HELOCs 

If you have equity in your home, you may be able to borrow against it. A home equity loan provides a fixed lump sum repaid over time, while a home equity line of credit (HELOC) provides a revolving line of credit. Both options carry risk, as your home serves as collateral.

High-cost options to use as a last resort 

Payday loans and title loans are other options you could use if you need funds to cover an emergency expense, but they often have the highest costs. Repayment could also be more challenging since you’ll usually have a shorter timeframe and less flexibility than you would with a personal loan or credit card.

What can you use an emergency loan for? 

An emergency loan, particularly an unsecured personal loan, can be used for a wide variety of urgent expenses. Most commonly, borrowers use these funds for unexpected costs such as major home repairs, vehicle maintenance, out-of-pocket medical bills, or family travel needs.

However, lenders typically place restrictions on how funds can be used. For example, personal loan funds generally cannot be used for post-secondary education costs, commercial or business investments, real estate purchases, or gambling. It’s important to review your lender’s specific terms and eligible use policies before applying.

Alternatives to emergency loans 

Borrowing usually comes with some type of cost, such as interest or risk, if you’re putting up collateral. Before you take an emergency loan, you may consider if there are other options available to you, such as the following: 

  • Emergency savings: If you have a rainy day fund, a personal emergency could be the perfect time to use it. There won’t be any additional costs associated with using it, but be careful about fully depleting your savings, and create a plan to replenish the account so you can be prepared for future emergencies. 
  • 0% introductory APR credit card: For people who can qualify for a new credit card, some offer introductory 0% APR periods on purchases that can last a year or more. This period of time could help you pay down a large expense without additional interest (assuming credit payments are accepted). The downsides are that regular APR will be applied to remaining balances once the promotional period ends, and you may not qualify for a high enough credit line depending on how much funding the emergency requires. 
  • Borrowing from family or friends: Be careful going this route since you don’t want to ruin any important relationships over money, but if you know someone who is in a position to help you financially, that could be worth exploring. Consider writing up a loan agreement so that there is no confusion or misunderstanding regarding the repayment plan.

FAQs about emergency loans

How quickly can you get an emergency loan? How quickly can you get an emergency loan?

Funding speed varies by lender, loan type, and application method. Online lenders and many traditional banks can process applications and make approval decisions quickly, often within the same business day or a few business days. Once approved and the agreement is signed, funds are typically deposited directly into your bank account. Exact timing depends on document verification and your receiving bank's processing times.

What credit score do you need for an emergency loan? What credit score do you need for an emergency loan?

The credit score you need to qualify for an emergency loan varies by lender. In general, if you have at least fair credit and meet lenders’ other requirements, you should be able to find emergency loan options. People in higher score tiers typically have a better chance of qualifying for the most favorable rates and terms, however.

How much can you borrow with an emergency loan? How much can you borrow with an emergency loan?

Loan amounts vary by lender and applicant qualifications. For example, Wells Fargo offers personal loans ranging from $3,000 to $100,000 for qualifying customers, subject to credit approval and income verification.

What documents do you need to apply for an emergency loan? What documents do you need to apply for an emergency loan?

To apply for an emergency loan, you typically need documentation that verifies your identity, address, income, and employment. Common requirements include a government-issued photo ID, recent W-2s, tax returns, pay stubs, or recent bank statements.

Do emergency loans hurt your credit score? Do emergency loans hurt your credit score?

Applying for a new loan typically triggers a hard credit inquiry, which may cause a minor, temporary dip in your credit score. However, establishing a track record of consistent, on-time monthly payments is an important factor that can help build and maintain a positive credit history over time.

Is an emergency loan better than using a credit card? Is an emergency loan better than using a credit card?

Whether an emergency loan is better than a credit card depends on your personal situation, how much you need to borrow, and the interest rate you can qualify for. A loan may be the less costly option if you’re approved for a lower APR than what a credit card charges, or if you need to borrow a large sum. However, for smaller emergency expenses, it may make more sense to use a credit card and pay it off gradually.

What is a debt consolidation loan?

Published October, 2026    8 min read
In this article
  • What is a debt consolidation loan?
  • How do debt consolidation loans work?
  • Types of debt consolidation loans
  • Do debt consolidation loans hurt your credit?
  • Pros and cons of debt consolidation loans
  • How to get a debt consolidation loan
  • Is a debt consolidation loan a good idea?
Key takeaways
  • A debt consolidation loan is a tool to help people refinance multiple high-interest debts into one personal, unsecured installment loan. 
  • Consolidating debt can help provide a more focused and sometimes less costly debt payoff approach if you are able to qualify for a loan with a lower interest rate and fair terms. 
  • There are other ways to consolidate debt, including tapping into your home equity or 401(k) balance, or applying for a balance transfer credit card.

If you have multiple debts or are carrying high-interest balances, a debt consolidation loan may be worth exploring. This type of loan transfers other debts into one loan to simplify your budget and potentially reduce the overall cost of borrowing. 

Learn more about how debt consolidation works, the different options available, and how to decide if it’s worth it for you.

What is a debt consolidation loan? 

A debt consolidation loan is a type of personal loan that allows borrowers to pay off multiple existing debt balances by rolling the balances into one loan payment. Some key benefits of a debt consolidation loan can include simplifying your debt payoff and lowering the overall cost of the debt by reducing interest charges. 

Repayment of the debt consolidation loan usually consists of fixed monthly installment payments for a set term.

How do debt consolidation loans work? 

A personal loan for debt consolidation usually provides a lump sum up front and is paid back with fixed installment payments. What sets debt consolidation apart is that the funds are specifically earmarked to refinance other existing debts such as credit card balances. Some lenders may even offer the option to make those debt payments on your behalf. 

If you can qualify for a personal debt consolidation loan with a lower interest rate than your existing debt’s interest rate, you may save money because you’ll pay less interest in the long term. 

Here’s an example. Let’s say you have one credit card with a $5,000 balance, another with an $8,000 balance, and a third with a $3,000 balance. They all have annual percentage rates (APRs) above 20%, so you’re not seeing much progress by making minimum payments. However, you have a good credit score, so you may be able to qualify for a debt consolidation loan with a lower APR that also covers those three cards. By making a fixed monthly payment, you can focus on a single loan payment and know it has an end date. 

(Note: This is a hypothetical example for illustrative purposes only. Actual rates and terms vary based on creditworthiness, loan amount, and lender.)

Types of debt consolidation loans 

Debt consolidation loans can be a type of personal loan, but there are other products that allow you to consolidate debt as well. The amount of your existing debt, the strength of your credit profile, and your repayment budget can help you decide which option is best for you.

Unsecured personal loans 

Most personal loans for debt consolidation are unsecured, meaning they are not backed by collateral. Instead, the lender assesses your eligibility by reviewing your credit history and verifying your ability to repay the loan. In most cases, interest rates and payments are fixed for the life of the loan.

Home equity loans and HELOCs 

Homeowners sometimes tap into their home equity to pay off high-interest debts. Two options for doing this are a home equity loan or a home equity line of credit (HELOC). A home equity loan is a second mortgage in which you take a lump-sum payment to pay your debts and then repay it with fixed payments. A HELOC is a revolving credit line that you can draw from as needed for a set period of time. Either approach can be risky because the home serves as collateral, so if you don’t meet your repayment obligations, you can face foreclosure.

Balance transfer credit cards 

Another option is a balance transfer credit card with a 0% introductory APR offer. Some of the most competitive balance transfer card 0% APR promotional periods are between one and two years. Balance transfers typically have a fee of 3% to 5% of the total transfer amount.

401(k) loans 

You may be able to borrow from your employer-sponsored 401(k) account, though most financial experts consider this a last-resort approach. The disadvantage is that when you use retirement funds to pay off debt, you could miss out on investment growth. You’ll also have to pay yourself back with interest by a set deadline. If you leave your job while you still owe on the 401(k) loan, you may owe income taxes and an early withdrawal penalty on the remaining balance.

Do debt consolidation loans hurt your credit? 

A debt consolidation loan won’t necessarily hurt your credit in the long term, though you may see a temporary drop in your credit score initially. How it affects your profile overall depends on how consistently you make on-time payments and whether you manage your paid-off accounts responsibly.

Short-term credit impacts 

Anytime you apply for a new line of credit, it can trigger a hard inquiry when the lender reviews your credit reports. This causes a small, temporary decrease in your credit score. New credit lines can also lower the average age of your credit, which is a factor in the major credit scoring algorithms. Short-term impacts typically level out over several months.

Long-term credit benefits 

Because you are using the debt consolidation loan funds to pay off your other debts, it can have long-term credit benefits. These loans can help you make faster progress with your debt payoff, especially if you can lower your interest rate. This drives down your utilization, or the amount of available credit you are using, which is a positive for your credit score. 

Regular payments that are made on time also benefit your score. Plus, because a personal loan for debt consolidation is an installment product, managing the repayment responsibly shows that you can handle a “mix” of credit, which is looked on favorably by the credit scoring models.

Pros and cons of debt consolidation loans 

Personal debt consolidation loans can be a good tool to help you conquer lingering, high-interest debt, but it’s important to consider both the potential advantages and drawbacks.

Pros 

  • Lower your interest rate and save money: Debt consolidation may reduce total borrowing cost when the new loan’s APR, fees, term, and total repayment are lower than the existing debts. One of the key ways to do that is to qualify for a consolidation loan that has a lower APR than the existing debt. 
  • Streamline your finances: Juggling multiple balances can be difficult to manage. If you’re only making minimum payments as well, it can be challenging to make progress. Consolidating debt into one payment simplifies your finances and lets you focus on a single bill. 
  • See faster progress on your debt payoff: If you’re paying less interest overall and you make all of your payments, you will be debt-free by the end of the loan term. You can speed up progress even more if you make larger payments to pay the loan off earlier.

Cons 

  • Potential fees: Some debt consolidation tools do have upfront fees such as origination fees on loans, closing costs on home equity products, and balance transfer fees on credit cards. These costs should be factored into your math when deciding if the consolidation is worthwhile. 
  • Requires discipline not to run up paid-off credit lines again: Once your credit cards have zero balances and you have one loan to pay back, if you start piling on new debt, you can end up back in the same position with a new loan on top. 
  • Must have strong credit to qualify for best rates: The most competitive interest rates usually go to borrowers with good to excellent credit. If you’re not in those tiers, it could be challenging to consolidate to a lower rate than you are paying, and that can remove much of the benefit.

How to get a debt consolidation loan 

You can get a debt consolidation loan by following these general steps. 

  1. Determine if you are eligible. Review your credit profile to see where you stand. Higher credit scores can help you qualify for more competitive rates. You’ll need to meet other lender criteria as well, including having a steady income source. 
  2. Figure out how much you need to borrow. List out your existing debts along with their APRs so you can figure out the loan amount you need. Consider paying off debts with higher interest rates if you can’t get a loan large enough to cover everything. 
  3. Calculate what monthly payment you can afford. Moving all of your debts into one loan may result in a significant monthly payment. If it’s higher than the total of each debt’s current minimum payment, make sure your budget can handle it. Explore different loan term lengths as well. Shorter terms typically have higher monthly payments but cost less in interest over the life of the loan, while longer terms may lower the monthly payment but accrue more interest. 
  4. Compare lender quotes. Once you know how much you want to borrow and what you can afford, you can compare loan options. Get a few offers and compare them side by side. 
  5. Apply. When you choose a lender, you can start the application process. Once approved, you can pay off your debts (or specify where the lender should direct payments if they are doing so on your behalf).

Is a debt consolidation loan a good idea? 

A debt consolidation loan can be a good idea for some borrowers. As with most financial decisions, it all depends on your specific situation, ability to qualify for favorable rates and terms, and whether you have a realistic repayment strategy in place. 

If you determine that you can qualify for a debt consolidation loan that would lower your interest rate and help you save money and accelerate repayment, it might be worth moving forward. The key is to make sure you can follow through on your repayment and avoid running up new balances that could put you in a worse situation than you were in originally.

FAQs about debt consolidation loans

What credit score do you need for a debt consolidation loan? What credit score do you need for a debt consolidation loan?

Each lender sets its own minimum score requirements, but you’ll typically need a “good” credit score, which generally starts at 670 under the FICO model. While some products are available for borrowers with lower scores, applicants with scores above 700 are more likely to qualify for competitive, single-digit interest rates.

Does debt consolidation close my credit cards? Does debt consolidation close my credit cards?

Paying off credit cards using a debt consolidation loan does not close your credit card accounts. It pays off your balances in full.

How much can you save with a debt consolidation loan? How much can you save with a debt consolidation loan?

The amount of money you can save with a debt consolidation loan depends on the type of debt you currently have and the loan’s terms. Crunch the numbers to see what a potential loan would cost you each month as well as over the life of the loan, and then compare it to your current repayment strategy. Note that longer-term loans cost more in interest than shorter-term loans.

What's the difference between debt consolidation and debt settlement? What's the difference between debt consolidation and debt settlement?

Debt consolidation is using a loan to pay off existing debts and then repaying that loan. Debt settlement is when a company negotiates on your behalf with your creditors to lower what you owe on your existing balances. However, the debt settlement strategy usually requires you to stop making payments for a period of time, which can significantly damage your credit score.

Does a debt consolidation loan get rid of my debt? Does a debt consolidation loan get rid of my debt?

No, a debt consolidation loan does not eliminate your debt. Instead, it replaces multiple existing balances with a single new loan. You are still responsible for paying back the full borrowed amount. However, consolidation can make repayment more manageable by streamlining your obligations into one monthly bill and potentially reducing your interest rate.

What is personal loan underwriting?

Published October, 2026    7 min read
In this article
  • What is loan underwriting?
  • Why do lenders underwrite personal loans?
  • What do underwriters look at?
  • How the personal loan underwriting process works
  • How long does personal loan underwriting take?
  • What are the possible underwriting outcomes?
  • How to prepare for underwriting
  • Getting through personal loan underwriting
Key takeaways
  • Personal loan underwriting is the process lenders use to determine the terms of the loan and whether an applicant qualifies for their product.
  • Loan underwriting can be done manually, automatically, or a combination of the two.
  • The main goal of underwriting is to see if a borrower is eligible for a loan based on their credit history and capacity to pay back the loan.

Whenever you apply for a personal loan, lenders have a process for deciding if you qualify and, if so, what rate to offer you. This process is known as underwriting. 

Learn more about how underwriting works, the criteria that underwriters use to make lending decisions, and how to prepare your finances so you’re in the best possible position before you apply for a loan.

What is loan underwriting?

Loan underwriting is a process lenders use to determine if a prospective borrower meets the requirements to qualify for a loan, and if so, the loan’s terms. Underwriting helps the lender assess the creditworthiness of the applicant by conducting a thorough review of the person’s financial background, credit history, and the capacity to repay the loan. 

Underwriting takes place after an applicant submits a loan application. Based on what is uncovered through underwriting, the lender decides if it will approve the loan and the loan’s terms.

Why do lenders underwrite personal loans?

Lenders underwrite personal loans to assess borrowers’ credit health and their ability to repay the loan. Most personal loans are unsecured, which means they’re not backed by collateral, so financial companies are taking a risk when they lend large sums of money. 

Underwriting helps minimize that risk by ensuring that borrowers meet specific minimum qualifications for approval. For example, a borrower’s credit score is one factor used to assess risk and predict future repayment behavior. While a credit score alone does not determine loan eligibility, applicants with higher credit scores may have a better chance of qualifying for a loan when all other underwriting criteria are the same.

What do underwriters look at?

Loan underwriters look at several factors to get a holistic view of an applicant’s financial situation. Lenders usually have their own evaluation framework for how different criteria are weighed and factored into the lending decision. In general, underwriters try to determine the following: 

  • Does this borrower’s track record indicate that they have been responsible with their credit lines? This question demonstrates why having strong credit is so important for being able to qualify for personal loans with competitive rates. 
  • Does this borrower have enough stable income to be able to pay back the loan? Even if you have strong credit, you may be denied by a lender if you don’t have ample income or if you’re carrying too much other debt. 

Underwriters look at a variety of documents and data to answer these questions, including credit reports, banking and financial records, and income and employment records.

Credit history and credit score

Personal loan underwriters will look at several criteria including your credit report and credit score to get a snapshot of your financial accounts and how you manage credit. Credit reports provide details on account behaviors and if you have had any past issues with creditors such as an account in default or a bankruptcy. The credit score reflects your most recent credit activity and account statuses. Depending on the credit score and other credit attributes, you may fall into different tiers of credit, which are poor, fair, good, or excellent.

Income and repayment ability

If you’re borrowing money and need to pay it back, you’ll need to have income. Lenders want to make sure that you have steady, reliable income streams. You may be asked for pay stubs, bank statements, or tax returns to prove it.

Debt-to-income (DTI) ratio

DTI is the percentage of your gross monthly income used to pay monthly debt. For instance, if you earn $5,000 per month, but your monthly debt costs $2,500, you have a 50% DTI. A higher ratio may affect how a lender evaluates your repayment capacity.

Collateral (for secured loans)

Some personal loans may be secured with collateral, most commonly an asset like your car. If you fail to repay as agreed, the lender may have the right to repossess or otherwise seek recovery from the collateral, subject to the loan agreement and applicable law.

Employment and financial stability

Not only do lenders want to see that you earn income, but they want to know that you’re employed or that you receive regular paychecks. This is why some underwriters ask to verify your employment. If you frequently change jobs or do gig work with unsteady income, it may require additional documentation or be more challenging to qualify for a personal loan.

How the personal loan underwriting process works

The personal loan underwriting process works mostly behind the scenes after you submit your application. In most cases, you have already shared identification, documentation, or access to your financial accounts, as well as permitted the lender to perform a credit check.

Once the underwriters take over the process, they will begin reviewing your application piece by piece. They will do a deep dive into your credit history by looking at one (or more) of your credit reports. Underwriters may also verify the other information that you self-reported in your application, such as your income and other debts. Using this information, the lender will calculate your debt-to-income ratio. 

Depending on the lender’s specific underwriting process, you may be asked to submit additional documentation along the way, such as if the lender needs more supporting evidence of your income or employment.

Depending on the lender, the underwriting process may be conducted using automated systems, manual review by an underwriter, or a combination of both.

How long does personal loan underwriting take?

Underwriting for personal loans can take anywhere from a few minutes to several business days. 

A few lenders market themselves as offering fast approvals and likely use automated underwriting to offer that faster turnaround. It’s common to expect underwriting to take between one and three days. More complex applications requiring additional documentation may slow down the process.

What are the possible underwriting outcomes?

After a personal loan goes through underwriting, there are generally three different outcomes. The loan is either fully approved, conditionally approved, or denied.

Here’s a closer look at each underwriting outcome and what it means for the borrower.

Approved

Getting through underwriting with an approval means that you met the lender’s qualifications. Once approved, the lender will generate a customized loan offer. The borrower will be able to review the offer and decide to move forward or not.

Conditional approval

When an underwriting process determines that a borrower seems eligible for a personal loan but needs another item or two checked off to move forward, the lender may give the loan “conditional approval.” In other words, the loan is approved as long as specific conditions are met. For example, the borrower may need to provide additional income or asset verification, such as a W-2 or bank statement.

Denied and the adverse action notice

If underwriting determines that the borrower does not meet the minimum requirements for approval, the loan is denied. Lenders have a legal obligation to explain in person, in writing, or electronically the reasons why the borrower was denied the loan.

How to prepare for underwriting

If you’re seeking a loan in the near future, you can take several steps to prepare for the underwriting process. The first is to check your credit report and credit score so you know where you stand. This also gives you a chance to correct errors or make improvements before you apply. 

Next, see if you can find out from the lender what types of documentation you will need to apply. Some examples could include a recent pay stub, a W-2, a tax return, or a bank statement. Once you have that list, you can begin to gather what you need for the application.

Getting through personal loan underwriting

Understanding how personal loan underwriting works is important as you compare lenders and assess your ability to qualify for various products. The main thing to remember is that your credit history and income are key factors in how lenders evaluate you. They can also impact the type of offers you receive. Once you’re ready to apply, be prepared to share documentation and respond to requests for additional information promptly to help your loan application process go smoothly.

FAQs about personal loan underwriting

What does it mean when a loan is in underwriting? What does it mean when a loan is in underwriting?

When a loan is in underwriting, it means that you have submitted your application and that the lender is doing their due diligence to make sure that you meet the qualifications for the loan.

How long does personal loan underwriting take? How long does personal loan underwriting take?

Personal loan underwriting timeframes vary depending on the lender. It can take anywhere from a few minutes to several days, but in most cases, lenders will decide in a business day or two.

What do underwriters look for when reviewing a loan? What do underwriters look for when reviewing a loan?

When underwriters review loan applications, they want to make sure the information provided by the applicant is accurate and truthful. They will then look into the applicant’s credit history and verify income, employment, and other aspects of the application.

What's the difference between conditional approval and full approval? What's the difference between conditional approval and full approval?

Conditional loan approval means the application is nearly approved, but the applicant must meet one or more outstanding requirements. A full approval means that the borrower meets the lender’s requirements and they will receive a loan offer.

Does underwriting affect your credit score? Does underwriting affect your credit score?

Underwriting may affect your credit score because the lender performs a hard inquiry, also known as a hard pull, on your credit report. This tells the credit bureaus that you have applied for credit, which can cause a temporary but minor drop in your credit score.

What's the difference between manual and automated underwriting? What's the difference between manual and automated underwriting?

Manual underwriting involves a human reviewing your application and investigating your financial background, whereas a technology platform performs automated underwriting for evaluating specific credit criteria and the ability to pay.

Can you speed up the underwriting process? Can you speed up the underwriting process?

You can speed up the underwriting process by filling out your application carefully, submitting the most recent necessary documents, uploading clear and legible digital files, and responding quickly to additional underwriting requests.

Key takeaways
  • A loan maturity date is the day when you are expected to make the final payment of an installment loan.
  • To determine a loan’s maturity date, take the loan’s start date and count the number of months in the loan’s term.
  • Knowing when a loan matures can help you plan, set repayment goals, and work toward a debt-free end to the loan.

When you take out a loan, it’s important to have a plan for paying it back and to know exactly how long of a commitment you're making. Step one is knowing your loan maturity date so you can adjust your budget accordingly and begin the countdown to paying off your loan.

What is a loan maturity date?

A loan maturity date is the day that you’re expected to make your final loan payment. It represents the end of your loan term and the day when your total balance, including principal, interest, and any fees, must be paid in full.

At the loan maturity date, assuming full payment is made, the financial agreement between the lender and borrower comes to an end. It is also an important milestone for your finances because it means you will have successfully paid off a debt. This has positive implications for your credit history and gives you back some budget to work on other financial goals.

Here’s what else you need to know about loan maturity dates and how they can impact your personal loan decisions and overall finances.

What does it mean when a loan matures?

Unlike revolving lines of credit like credit cards that you can use again and again, installment loans have start and end dates. When a loan matures, it means that it has reached its endpoint.

At loan maturity, the expectation is that the borrower will make their last payment, thus fulfilling the debt obligation they originally agreed to when they took the loan.

Why your loan maturity date matters

The loan maturity date matters because it gives borrowers a finish line to strive toward. Knowing this date in advance can help you plan. During the payoff period, you’ll know that you need to leave room in your budget each month for the required installment payment.

Knowing the loan’s end date is in sight may help you stay motivated and celebrate milestones along the way. You can also look ahead and plan for what you may do with the extra cash flow as your maturity date approaches.

A loan’s maturity date is also important in the context of other financial goals you may have. For instance, if you know you want to buy a home in the next three years, choosing a loan that matures in five years could impact your mortgage application.

How does a loan maturity date work?

From the day you accept a loan offer, your loan maturity date will be known to you as the day that your final payment is due. If you have a loan term of 36 months, for example, the loan maturity date will be the day when your 36th payment is due.

Where to find your maturity date

Your loan maturity date can be found in a number of places. To start, it will appear in your loan agreement. You may also see it listed on your monthly account statements, or when you log into your online account or loan app. Lenders may use charts or tools that illustrate your loan payoff progress.

What happens if you miss the maturity date

Failing to pay off your loan by the maturity date means that you did not meet the loan agreement’s terms. Depending on the lender, this could result in late fees or additional interest charges, and it could have consequences such as a negative impact on your credit score. The loan could also go into default or be moved to collections.

Maturity date vs. loan term vs. payment due date

While all related, the terms “maturity date,” “loan term,” and “payment due date” are different.

  • Loan term refers to the length or duration of the loan, so a term might be 24 months, for example.
  • The maturity date marks the end of the loan term.
  • The payment due date is when your installment payment must be made each month. (The final payment due date in the loan term is the loan maturity date.)

How your loan term shapes your maturity date

The maturity date is determined based on the start date of the loan and the loan term. The maturity date is the loan’s endpoint. Here’s an example:

Meg took out a five-year loan and signed her loan agreement on May 1, 2026. She would then make 60 monthly payments until May 1, 2031, which is the loan maturity date.

To figure out the maturity date on any loan, just follow this formula: Loan start date + number of months in the loan term = maturity date.

Assuming that you make all of your monthly installment payments, you will fully pay off your loan when the loan reaches its maturity date.

How maturity dates differ by loan type

Depending on the type of loan, your maturity date could be sometime in the near future or a long while away. In general, the further away your maturity date is, the more interest you will pay over the life of the loan.

Here are some different types of loans and what their maturity dates typically look like:

  • Personal loan: These installment loans are usually between two and seven years in length (24 to 84 months).
  • Auto loan: Most auto loans are three to six years (36 to 72 months).
  • Mortgage: The most common home loans are 30-year fixed terms, but there are also 15-year loans and other customized terms available.

Credit cards don’t have a maturity date because they’re revolving lines of credit. In other words, there is no final payment due date because you can borrow from them repeatedly against your available credit. Additionally, your payments can fluctuate month to month.

Amortization and your maturity date

Amortization refers to how your loan payments are spread out and allocated over the life of a loan. Even though your loan payment is fixed, you are actually paying different amounts of principal and interest during the term. With most loans, you pay more interest in the earlier portion of the loan term.

The end of the amortization schedule is when the final payment is due, and both principal and interest payments have been paid in full. This is also known as the maturity date.

Can you pay off a loan before its maturity date?

With most loans, you should have the option to accelerate payments or pay off the loan before it reaches the maturity date. Paying off your loan early can reduce the amount of interest you pay and lower your overall borrowing costs.

It’s a good idea to review your loan agreement, as lenders may charge a prepayment penalty or other fees if you pay off the loan before the maturity date.

Aim for a maturity date that fits your life

When considering a loan, the loan’s maturity date is a key factor. Knowing the maturity date can help you plan and adjust your budget, and it can give you an end date to work toward.

Once your loan matures and you complete the payoff, you can feel good about meeting your obligation and freeing up that money for other priorities.

FAQs about loan maturity dates

Can I change the maturity date on my loan? Can I change the maturity date on my loan?

Maturity dates on loans are typically fixed. However, you could change the date if you refinance the loan or modify it. You may also be able to pay off the loan earlier.

Do all loans have a maturity date? Do all loans have a maturity date?

While installment loans have a maturity date, some loans operate as lines of credit that revolve. Because borrowing with such products, including credit cards, is open-ended, there is no specific end date.

Is the maturity date the same as my final payment date? Is the maturity date the same as my final payment date?

Yes, the maturity date on a loan is also the final payment due date. Once the loan reaches maturity and you make your last payment, the loan agreement is complete.

What happens to my credit when a loan matures? What happens to my credit when a loan matures?

Successfully repaying the loan can contribute positively to your credit history, but the effect on your score may vary. Successfully repaying an installment loan demonstrates that you handled a debt responsibly. Making late payments, missing payments, or becoming delinquent on the loan may negatively impact your credit.

Does a maturity date mean the full balance is due that day? Does a maturity date mean the full balance is due that day?

Yes, a loan’s maturity date means that any remaining principal, accrued interest, and applicable fees are due in full.

Can a loan be extended past its maturity date? Can a loan be extended past its maturity date?

You may be able to work with your lender to extend a loan past its maturity date, but it usually requires a loan modification or refinancing. Lenders may also offer forbearance or deferment.

Wells Fargo Credit Close-Up® Service Addendum to the Wells Fargo Online Access Agreement

Effective as of 11/16/2021

This Addendum ("Addendum") and the Wells Fargo Online Access Agreement ("OAA") contain the terms and conditions governing your use of the Credit Close-Up® service. If we make changes to this Addendum, we will update the Addendum on the website. We will notify you of changes following the procedures specified in the OAA. If there is a conflict between this Addendum and the OAA, this Addendum will control with regard to the Credit Close-Up® service.

Please read this Addendum carefully. By agreeing to this Addendum, or by accessing or using the Credit Close-Up® service, you are agreeing to the terms and conditions of this Addendum and the OAA. This Addendum and the OAA include, among other things:

  • your consent to Wells Fargo accessing and using your consumer report
  • your consent to Wells Fargo sharing information in your consumer report with its affiliates, such as Wells Fargo Advisors
  • our obligations to you
  • your obligations as a user of the Credit Close-Up® service
  • your agreement to use binding arbitration, and to waive the right to a trial by jury, for most disputes with Experian, CSIdentity, and us arising under this Addendum or relating to the Credit Close-Up® service
  • your waiver of class-action rights
  • limitations on liability to you

Your agreement to this Addendum is essential to our agreement to provide the Credit Close-Up® service to you. If this Addendum is unacceptable to you at any time, you should terminate your enrollment in the Credit Close-Up® service.

1. Definitions

Except as otherwise provided in this Addendum, terms defined in the OAA have the same meaning in this Addendum. In addition, in this Addendum:

  • "CSIdentity" refers to CSIdentity Corporation, an Experian service provider that facilitates our provision of the Credit Close-Up® service to you.
  • "Experian" refers to Experian Information Solutions, Inc., a consumer reporting agency.
  • "FICO® Scores" refers to credit scores created by Fair Isaac Corporation
  • "We," "Us," "Our," and "Wells Fargo" refer to Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
  • "You" and "your" refer to you as the person entering into this Addendum.

2. Eligibility

To enroll in the Credit Close-Up® service, you must be a Wells Fargo account holder enrolled in Wells Fargo Online®, a resident of the United States (or a United States territory), and at least 18 years old. FICO® Scores will be delivered only to the Wells Fargo account holder and only if a FICO® Score is available for the Wells Fargo account holder. In some circumstances, such as if your account is closed, charged-off, or recently-opened, or if we are unable to verify your identity, you may not be eligible to receive a FICO® Score through the Credit Close-Up® service.

3. Authorization to obtain consumer report and credit score

By enrolling in the Credit Close-Up® service and agreeing to this Addendum, you are providing Wells Fargo and its service providers, including CSIdentity, with "written instructions" in accordance with the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act and any other applicable laws to access and use consumer report information about you from one or more consumer reporting agencies. You authorize us to access and use this information, including your FICO® Score, to present you with an overview of your credit profile, to present you with credit and financial guidance, to offer products and services that may be of interest to you, for internal analytics, and for other purposes related to your relationship with us. In connection with the Credit Close-Up® service, we may use your Social Security number and other personal information to access your consumer report and to verify your identity.

Obtaining your FICO® Score through the Credit Close-Up® service results in a soft credit inquiry on your credit report. This soft credit inquiry does not affect your FICO® Score.

4. Consent to sharing of consumer report and credit score information

By enrolling in the Credit Close-Up® service and agreeing to this Addendum, you consent to us sharing the consumer report information that we obtain about you in connection with the Credit Close-Up® service, including your FICO® Score, with our affiliates, including Wells Fargo Advisors. As outlined in our Privacy Policy, you may limit our sharing of some information about you with our affiliates. Please note, however, that limiting our sharing of information about you with our affiliates consistent with our Privacy Policy will not terminate your enrollment in the Credit Close-Up® service or revoke your consent to share the consumer report information we obtain about you in connection with the Credit Close-Up® service with our affiliates. You must terminate your enrollment in the Credit Close-Up® service if you want us to stop obtaining new consumer report information about you in connection with the Credit Close-Up® service.

5. FICO® Credit Score

The FICO® Score presented to you through the Credit Close-Up® service is for your educational, non-commercial, and personal benefit and use only. The FICO® Score presented to you may not be the credit score we use to make account opening or credit decisions, and we may use other FICO® Scores and other information to review an application for a credit or deposit account.

Your FICO® Score reflects a general snapshot of your credit profile at a specific point in time, and it can vary from month to month. The credit file used to create your FICO® Score is updated continuously, and the FICO® Score presented to you through the Credit Close-Up® service may not reflect the most current data in your credit file.

6. Arbitration agreement and class-action waiver

Please read this section carefully as it affects your rights.

The Credit Close-Up® service is part of Wells Fargo Online® and subject to the OAA, and with regard to Wells Fargo, the OAA governs the arbitration of any disputes relating in any way to this Addendum or the Credit Close-Up® service.

By enrolling in the Credit Close-Up® service and agreeing to this Addendum, and pursuant to the Federal Arbitration Act, you also agree that any dispute between you and Experian or its service provider, CSIdentity, relating in any way to the Credit Close-Up® service or this Addendum will, at your election or at the election of Experian or CSIdentity, be resolved through binding arbitration and not through litigation in any court of general jurisdiction. ESIGN Consent to Use Electronic Records and Signatures (ESIGN Consent)

As part of your relationship with us, we want to ensure you have all of the information you need to effectively manage your accounts. Our goal is to provide you with as many options as possible for receiving your account documents. We are required by law to give you certain information "in writing" – which means you are entitled to receive it on paper. However, with your prior consent, we may instead provide this information to you electronically. We also need your general consent to use electronic records and signatures throughout our relationship with you. So, before you use any of our Electronic Services (as defined below), you must review and consent to the terms outlined below.

In this ESIGN Consent:

  • "We," "us," "our" and "Wells Fargo" means Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., Wells Fargo Advisors, and each and every current and future affiliate of Wells Fargo & Company.
  • "You" and "your" means the person giving this ESIGN Consent, and also each additional account owner, authorized signer, authorized representative, delegate, product owner and/or service user identified on any Wells Fargo Product that you apply for, use or access.
  • "Communications" means each disclosure, notice, agreement, fee schedule, statement, record, document, and other information we provide to you, or that you sign, submit, or agree to at our request.
  • "Electronic Service" means each and every product and service we offer that you apply for, use, administer or access using the Internet, a website, email, messaging services (including text messaging), and/or software applications (including applications for mobile or hand-held devices), either now or in the future.
  • "Wells Fargo Product" means each and every account, product, or service we offer that you apply for, own, use, administer or access, either now or in the future. Wells Fargo Products include Electronic Services.
  • The words "include" and "including," when used at the beginning of a list of one or more items, indicates that the list contains examples; the list is not exclusive or exhaustive, the items in the list are only illustrations, and the items are not the only possible items that could appear in the list.

Note:  If you click on any hyperlink provided for convenience below, be sure to come back to this page to finish reading this ESIGN Consent.

1. Your consent to use electronic records and signatures; Choosing to receive Communications electronically or in writing; Certain information must still be provided in writing.

In our sole discretion, the Communications we provide to you, or that you sign or agree to at our request, may be in electronic form ("Electronic Records"). View additional examples of types of Communications that we may send as Electronic Records under this consent. We may also use electronic signatures and obtain them from you as part of our transactions with you.

Electronic Records may be delivered to you in a variety of ways. These various delivery methods are described in our Online Access Agreement and in other agreements we may have with you from time to time. In some cases, you will be able to choose whether to receive certain Communications electronically, or on paper, or both. We will provide you with instructions on how to make those choices when they are available.

We may always, in our sole discretion, provide you with any Communication via paper, even if you have chosen to receive it electronically.

Sometimes the law, or our agreement with you, requires you to give us a written notice. You must still provide these notices to us on paper, unless we specifically tell you in another Communication how you may deliver that notice to us electronically.

There are certain Communications that by law we are not permitted to deliver to you electronically, even with your consent. So long as required by law, we will continue to deliver those Communications to you in writing. However, if the law changes in the future and permits any of those Communications to be delivered as Electronic Records, this ESIGN Consent will automatically cover those Communications as well.

We will continue to provide your tax statements on paper unless you separately elect to receive them electronically (if available).

2. Your option to receive paper copies.

If we provide Electronic Records to you, and you want a paper copy, you may contact the appropriate customer service unit and request a paper version. You will find the appropriate contact information in the account statement or agreement for the Wells Fargo Product related to the Electronic Record. You may have to pay a fee for the paper copy unless charging a fee is prohibited by applicable law. Please refer to the applicable statement or agreement for any fee that may apply for paper copies.

3. Your consent covers all Wells Fargo Products; Privacy Policies.

Your consent covers all Communications relating to any Wells Fargo Product. Your consent remains in effect until you give us notice that you are withdrawing it.

From time to time, you may seek to obtain a new Wells Fargo Product from us. When you do, we may remind you that you have already given us your consent to use Electronic Records and signatures. If you decide not to use Electronic Records and signatures in connection with the new product or service, your decision does not mean you have withdrawn this consent for any other Wells Fargo Product.

You agree that we may satisfy our obligation to provide you with an annual copy of our Privacy Policy by keeping it available for review on www.wellsfargo.com, or, with prior notice to you, on another website where we offer Electronic Services.

4. You may withdraw your consent at any time; Consequences of withdrawing consent; How to give notice of withdrawal.

You have the right to withdraw your consent at any time. Please be aware, however, that withdrawal of consent may result in the termination of:

  • your access to our Electronic Services, including online banking, and
  • your ability to use certain Wells Fargo Products.

Your withdrawal of consent will become effective after we have had a reasonable opportunity to act upon it.

If you are receiving online account statements, the termination will cause paper statements to be mailed to you via the U.S. Postal Service or other courier. Depending on the specific Wells Fargo Product, if you withdraw consent we may charge higher or additional fees for that product or for services related to it. Please refer to the applicable agreement for any fee that may apply.

To withdraw your consent:

  • If you are enrolled in online banking, you must contact us at 1-800-956-4442.
  • If you are not enrolled in online banking, you must contact us at 1-800-869-3557.
  • For Brokerage Services with Access Online, you must contact the Investment Contact Center at 1-877-879-2495.

Deaf or Hard of Hearing Customers

We accept all relay calls, including 711.

5. You must keep your email or electronic address current with us.

You must promptly notify us of any change in your email or other electronic address. Sign on to Wells Fargo Online® to update your contact information and change the email address on record for you. There may be other, special Wells Fargo Products for which we provide separate instructions to update your email or other electronic address.

6. Hardware and software you will need.

To receive Electronic Records, you must have access to:

  • a Current Version (defined below) of an Internet browser we support,
  • a connection to the Internet,
  • a Current Version of a program that accurately reads and displays PDF files (such as Adobe® Acrobat® Reader),
  • a computer and an operating system capable of supporting all of the above. You will also need a printer if you wish to print out and retain records on paper, and electronic storage if you wish to retain records in electronic form, and
  • an active email address.

In some cases, you may also need a specific brand or type of device that can support a particular software application, including an application intended for particular mobile or handheld devices.

By "Current Version," we mean a version of the software that is currently being supported by its publisher. The following link includes more information on the browsers we currently support and related system requirements: Technical Requirements.

You should check the Technical Requirements page occasionally for updates on supported software. From time to time, we may offer services or features that require that your Internet browser be configured in a particular way, such as permitting the use of JavaScript or cookies. If we detect that your Internet browser is not properly configured, we will provide you with a notice and advice on how to update your configuration.

We reserve the right to discontinue support of a Current Version of software if, in our sole opinion, it suffers from a security flaw or other flaw that makes it unsuitable for use with Electronic Services.

7. Changes to hardware or software requirements.

If our hardware or software requirements change, and that change would create a material risk that you would not be able to access or retain your Electronic Records, we will give you notice of the revised hardware or software requirements. Continuing to use Electronic Services after receiving notice of the change is reaffirmation of your consent.

8. Your enrollment in Electronic Services using our equipment.

If you utilize an Electronic Service through one of our customer service representatives or using our equipment, your enrollment may not be complete until you take additional action. We will advise you, at the time of your enrollment, of any additional action you must take. If you take the required action, it is an affirmation of your consent to use Electronic Records and signatures under the terms of this ESIGN Consent.

9. Communications in languages other than English.

Please note, we may be unable to fulfill and service Wells Fargo Products in a language other than English. Future Communications may be in English only. If you are not fluent in English, you should consider obtaining the services of an interpreter or taking other steps to ensure you understand the transaction before entering into it and to have any future English Communications explained to you.

Our Communications are produced in English. For your convenience, we will provide a Spanish translation when available. You agree that the English version is always the controlling Communication.

By providing your consent, you are also confirming that you have the hardware and software described above, that you are able to receive and review Electronic Records, and that you have an active email account. You are also confirming that you are authorized to, and do, consent on behalf of all the other account owners, authorized signers, authorized representatives, delegates, product owners and/or service users identified with your Wells Fargo Products  .

Additional examples of Electronic Records covered by this ESIGN Consent include:

  1. This ESIGN Consent and any amendments;
  2. Our Online Access Agreement, other service or user agreements for online access to our Electronic Services, and all amendments to any of these agreements;
  3. All of the Communications related to any Wells Fargo Product, except for those excluded by the terms of this ESIGN Consent;
  4. All of the periodic account and activity statements, disclosures and notices we provide to you concerning your Wells Fargo Products;
  5. Brokerage disclosures, agreements, statements, trade confirmations, tax reporting statements (if you elect electronic delivery), shareholder notices, prospectuses, Service Notices and Performance Reports regarding accounts, products and services offered by or through Wells Fargo Advisors;
  6. Any notice or disclosure regarding fees or assessments of any kind, including late fees, overdraft fees, over limit fees, and returned item fees;
  7. Notices of amendments to any of your agreements with us; and
  8. Other disclosures and notices that we are legally required to provide to you, or choose to provide to you in our discretion.

Investment and Insurance Products are:

  • Not Insured by the FDIC or Any Federal Government Agency
  • Not a Deposit or Other Obligation of, or Guaranteed by, the Bank or Any Bank Affiliate
  • Subject to Investment Risks, Including Possible Loss of the Principal Amount Invested

FACTS

WHAT DOES WELLS FARGO BANK, N.A.
DO WITH YOUR PERSONAL INFORMATION?

Why?

Financial companies choose how they share your personal information. Federal law gives consumers the right to limit some but not all sharing. Federal law also requires us to tell you how we collect, share, and protect your personal information. Please read this notice carefully to understand what we do.

What?

The types of personal information we collect and share depend on the product or service you have with us. This information can include:

  • Social Security number and employment information
  • Account balances and transaction history
  • Credit history and income

How?

All financial companies need to share customers’ personal information to run their everyday business. In the section below, we list the reasons financial companies can share their customers’ personal information; the reasons Wells Fargo chooses to share; and whether you can limit this sharing.

Please note:  If you are a new customer, we can begin sharing your information 30 days from the date we sent this notice. When you are no longer our customer, we can continue to share your information as described in this notice. 

However, you can contact us at any time to limit our sharing.

To limit direct marketing

  • To limit our direct marketing to you by mail or telephone, call 1-833-714-3492 — our menu will prompt you through your choices

  • Online and mobile banking customers - Sign on and from the My Profile or Profile menu, select Change Privacy Preferences or Privacy Preferences.

Please note: A Do Not Call election is effective for five years, or while you are an active consumer customer, if longer than five years. The Do Not Mail election is effective for three years. You may continue to receive marketing information in regular account mailings and statements, when you visit us online or at an ATM. You may also be contacted to service your account or participate in surveys.

Questions?

Call 1-833-714-3490 or go to wellsfargo.com/privacy-security

Who we are

Who is providing this notice?

Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. This notice applies to Choice Privileges®Mastercard Credit Card accounts. Other Wells Fargo accounts are covered by a different privacy notice provided in connection with those accounts.

What we do

How does Wells Fargo protect my personal information?

To protect your personal information from unauthorized access and use, we use security measures that comply with federal law. These measures include computer safeguards and secured files and buildings. For more information visit wellsfargo.com/privacy-security.

How does Wells Fargo collect my personal information?

We collect your personal information, for example, when you:

  • Open an account or provide employment information
  • Apply for a loan or use your credit or debit card
  • Give us your income information

We also collect your personal information from others, such as credit bureaus, affiliates, or other companies.

Why can’t I limit all sharing?

Federal law gives you the right to limit only:

  • Sharing for affiliates’ everyday business purposes - information about your creditworthiness
  • Affiliates from using your information to market to you
  • Sharing for nonaffiliates to market to you

State laws and individual companies may give you additional rights to limit sharing.See below for more on your rights under state law.

What happens when I limit sharing for an account I hold jointly with someone else?

  • If you limit sharing with affiliates, your choices will apply individually unless you tell us otherwise. Any account holder may express a privacy preference on behalf of the other joint account holders
  • If you limit sharing with nonaffiliates, your choices will apply to everyone on your account
Definitions

Affiliates

Companies related by common ownership or control. They can be financial and non-financial companies.

Nonaffiliates

Companies not related by common ownership or control. They can be financial and non-financial companies.

  • Nonaffiliates we share with can include the retailer named on your account, its affiliates, and its service providers

Joint marketing

A formal agreement between nonaffiliated financial companies that together market financial products or services to you.

  • Wells Fargo doesn't jointly market

Marketing calls/texts or artificial or prerecorded voice message calls may be made to residential or cellular phone numbers that appear on the Wells Fargo Do Not Call list with the appropriate consent.

For more information contact us at 1-800-869-3557; PrivacyCenter@wellsfargo.com, or Wells Fargo, P.O. Box 5110, Sioux Falls, SD 57117-5110. If you would like more information regarding this Nevada law, contact: Bureau of Consumer Protection, Office of the Nevada Attorney General, 100 N. Carson Street, Carson City, NV 89701; 702-486-3132; AgInfo@ag.nv.gov.

State Law: We follow applicable state law where it provides you with additional privacy protections.

Vermont residents: We will not disclose information about your creditworthiness to our affiliates other than as permitted by Vermont law, unless you authorize us to make those disclosures.
